# Vancouver Daily News
> **A California driver was ticketed at 208 km/h near Squamish, and police impounded the car.**

**What You Need to Know:** A California driver was ticketed at 208 km/h near Squamish, and police impounded the car. Fare and household charges are lined up for 2027, and a woman died in a Squamish boating tragedy after going out in floodwater. Surrey is pulling its development company into city hall, and the children's representative wants a youth mental-health law.

### Top Stories
**California man ticketed for going 208 km/h on Sea-to-Sky Highway: Global BC**
A 22-year-old man visiting from California was ticketed after RCMP recorded him at 208 km/h in a 90 km/h zone on the Sea-to-Sky Highway near Squamish earlier this month. CBC reports he was allegedly driving that speed in a BMW, which was impounded for seven days. The stop is a police enforcement case, not a court finding. Source: [globalnews.ca](https://globalnews.ca/news/12164487/california-man-ticketed-excessive-speeding-sea-to-sky-highway/) Source: [cbc.ca](https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/british-columbia/sea-to-sky-highway-speeding-impound-rcmp-9.7434141?cmp=rss)

**Here's what B.C. laws and fees are changing in 2027: Daily Hive Vancouver**
TransLink fares are set to rise 2 per cent in 2027, after 5 per cent increases. Daily Hive reports a one-zone cash fare would go from $3.50 to $3.55, a one-zone Compass fare from $2.85 to $3.00, and a one-zone monthly pass from $117.20 to $119.55, with the board voting the exact increase each year before it takes effect. A Metro Vancouver draft budget, not yet adopted, would lift water, sewer, garbage and parks charges from $897 to $914, a $17 or 1.9 per cent increase, about $76 a month; the previous board deferred the vote, and the new board's first meeting is Nov. 27. The maximum allowable rent increase for 2027 is 2.2 per cent, and landlords decide whether to use it. BC Hydro's 2027 rate increase is expected April 1, 2027, with its application due in February; its 2026 increase was 3.75 per cent, and it is seeking a two-year optional fixed-bill pilot from Nov. 1, 2027 to Oct. 31, 2029. BC Ferries' average annual fare increase is capped at 3.2 per cent until March 2028. The Bank of Canada raised its policy rate on Oct. 28 from 2.25 per cent to 2.5 per cent; Ratehub.ca reported variable rates up 25 basis points and the average five-year fixed rate up 43 basis points to 4.99 per cent, with the next decision on Dec. 9, 2026. Premier Lorne Doerkson has promised a $1,000 income-tax cut for families, low-income earners and seniors; that is a campaign promise, not a law in force. Source: [dailyhive.com](https://dailyhive.com/vancouver/2027-laws-fees-changes-bc-residents)

**Woman who died in Squamish boating tragedy loved life, animals, family says: Global BC**
A woman died in a Squamish boating tragedy, Global BC reports. Friends say she was Femke Visser, a local horse guide and dogsled guide. They say she had gone out with neighbours to help animals and people stranded by the floodwater. Source: [globalnews.ca](https://globalnews.ca/news/12164610/woman-died-squamish-boating-tragedy-loved-life-animals/)

### City & Province
**Likely end to B.C. NDP housing reforms doesn't mean cities will revert to picket-fence neighbourhoods: Vancouver Sun**
Premier Lorne Doerkson has pledged to rescind Bill 44, the 2023 NDP law that required municipalities over 5,000 residents to allow up to four units on a single-family lot and six near transit. Port Coquitlam Mayor Brad West introduced a motion this week directing staff to disregard new applications for those projects, pending clarification of the province's planned changes. A Vancouver Sun column reports that many mayors want land-use power back, while most say they still want density on their own terms and do not want to lose federal housing-accelerator funding, which requires communities over 10,000 to allow at least four units per property. Burnaby was approved for $44.1 million and has received $32.9 million; the city said Tuesday it is well-positioned for a final advance of about $11.2 million in 2027, subject to federal review, and does not anticipate the Bill 44 changes will stop it delivering housing. Mayor Mike Hurley, re-elected last month, said in an open letter this month that Burnaby led the opposition to a one-size-fits-all approach that ignored local infrastructure, schools and parking. The column notes Global News reported Toronto lost $10 million after limiting multiplexes to some neighbourhoods. Port Coquitlam did not get accelerator funding; West wrote Tuesday that the law worked against the city's townhome market, and new West Vancouver Mayor Kirk LaPointe said council heard both an appetite for change and an appetite to preserve neighbourhood character. Source: [vancouversun.com](https://vancouversun.com/opinion/columnists/bc-conservatives-seem-set-to-scrap-ndp-housing-reforms-that-doesnt-mean-bc-cities-will-revert-to-picket-fence-neighbourhoods-of-last-century)

**Surrey to audit how truck parking, retail cannabis permits awarded: CBC**
Surrey city council has ordered a trio of new forensic audits into decisions by the previous administration, CBC reports. The reviews include how that administration awarded retail cannabis licences. They also cover permits to operate truck parking on city-owned land. Source: [cbc.ca](https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/british-columbia/surrey-forensic-audits-9.7434551?cmp=rss) Source: [cbc.ca](https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/british-columbia/surrey-forensic-audits-9.7434551)

### The Closer Look
**New premier must overhaul youth mental-health system: Representative: Vancouver Sun**
B.C.'s representative for children and youth, Jennifer Charlesworth, said Tuesday she wants the new Conservative government to change how youth mental health works in the province. She is asking for a stand-alone Youth Mental Health Act, which would be a first in Canada, or a youth-specific section in the Mental Health Act. She called the current Act archaic and said it focuses almost exclusively on adults. "The mental-health concerns of young people have been growing significantly," she said. "The most important thing for a new minister to understand is children and youth are different from adults."

She said the Act largely concentrates on detaining people in a crisis. She wants an expanded set of publicly funded, voluntary services that could stabilize young people in the community. Postmedia News reported this week that youth mental-health problems are rising and that young people frequently face long wait-lists. Charlesworth said that matches what parents tell her: "They asked for help over and over and over again, and they weren't able to access it. And then (their kids' mental health) got really serious."

Mandate letters from Premier Lorne Doerkson for Health Minister Ryan Peterson and the rest of cabinet were expected to be made public this week. Charlesworth plans to write to the ministers with her requested changes after she reads those letters.

She had already lobbied the previous NDP government. She said that government introduced some positive voluntary options, including Foundry Centres, but that demand and need still outstrip available services. Her recent report found an average of 1,600 teens ages 12 to 17 were involuntarily detained under the Mental Health Act each year between 2020 and 2025. That was 14 times the rate of youth detained by the justice system.

During the campaign, the Conservatives promised to review the Mental Health Act, reduce wait times and expand early services. Charlesworth said she supports those directions. She is more worried about a platform pledge to promote anti-drug education in schools, which she said has failed in the past, and about a promise to increase mandatory care for people who may be a risk to themselves or others. Too often, she said, community services are not there on release, and evidence suggests forced treatment can jeopardize long-term recovery and survival. "We need to build out a voluntary system before we rely too heavily on an involuntary one," she said.

Ania Wysocka, founder of Rootd, a panic-attack and anxiety-relief app she created in Victoria after a panic attack in university, said a separate Act would organize care more clearly because young people's needs differ from adults'. Anxiety, she said, can often show up first in the teen and early adult years. When young people are folded into a system built mainly around adults, she said, the focus tends to be crisis and treatment, "when what many of them need most is support early on, before things escalate." Source: [vancouversun.com](https://vancouversun.com/health/local-health/new-premier-must-overhaul-youth-mental-health-system-representative)

### Also Today
**Heavy rains, storm surge, high tides cause 'real drama' along B.C.'s coast: CityNews Vancouver**
CityNews reports Environment Canada warns of as much as 225 millimetres of rain along much of the coast before the end of the day, as a king tide coincides with storm surge and high tides. Source: [vancouver.citynews.ca](https://vancouver.citynews.ca/2026/11/25/heavy-rains-storm-surge-high-tides-cause-real-drama-along-b-c-s-coast/)

**Suspected North Korean computer programmers did contract work for B.C. government: CBC**
CBC reports suspected North Korean computer programmers did contract work for the B.C. government. Source: [cbc.ca](https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/suspected-north-korean-computer-programmers-british-columbia-government-9.7433830)

**B.C. mining expertise draws Epiroc electrification investment: Business in Vancouver**
Swedish mining-equipment maker Epiroc has opened a plant in Port Coquitlam, Business in Vancouver reports. Source: [biv.com](https://www.biv.com/news/resources-agriculture/bc-mining-expertise-draws-epiroc-electrification-investment-13049305)

### Getting Around
A vehicle incident on Highway 91 in Delta, near the end of the bridge, has the right lane blocked; DriveBC's last update was 6:08 a.m., with a next update at 7:00 a.m. Highway 1 is closed from 256th Street in Langley to Lefeuvre Road in Abbotsford until Dec. 31, with a detour and eastbound traffic shifted south of the median, and separate overnight Highway 1 work runs to Dec. 15 with a 60 km/h limit and a single lane each way. The Queensborough Bridge on Highway 91A is down to one lane each direction overnight, and weekday bridge work on Highway 7B in Port Coquitlam, between United Boulevard and Shaughnessy Street, runs 7 a.m. to 5 p.m. with width restrictions. Environment Canada has a yellow rainfall warning for Sea to Sky from Squamish to Whistler and a coastal flooding statement for Vancouver; it is 11 degrees and light rain now, with 10 to 15 mm this afternoon, heavy rain of 30 mm tonight and southeast gusts to 80 km/h, then a Thursday high of 12 with 10 to 15 mm and a thunder risk, and a Friday high of 10 with periods of rain. Source: [drivebc.ca](https://www.drivebc.ca/) Source: [weather.gc.ca](https://weather.gc.ca/rss/weather/49.245_-123.115_e.xml)

### Sports
**How to watch tonight's streaming-only Canucks-Red Wings game: Daily Hive Vancouver**
The Canucks visit the Detroit Red Wings tonight at Little Caesars Arena, with puck drop at 7:30 p.m. Eastern; Inside The Rink lists Vancouver at 6-19-1 and 13 points, and Detroit at 8-12-3 and 19 points. The game is only on Amazon Prime Video's Wednesday Night Hockey, not traditional television; Prime members pay nothing extra, and Daily Hive lists membership at $9.99 a month, $99 a year, or $4.99 a month and $49 a year for students after a six-month trial. It is one of two Canucks games on Prime this season, with the other Dec. 16 against the Anaheim Ducks, and nine further games are streaming-only on Sportsnet+, two of them already played, for 11 games off traditional television. Cole Reinhardt, claimed off waivers this week, skated on a fourth line with Paul Cotter and Jacob Quillan. NHL.com says Brock Boeser has 16 points, 4 goals and 12 assists, on a career-long 11-game point streak. Detroit plays its first game since trading Dylan Larkin; the return included Michael Hage, Kirby Dach, Samuel Montembeault and draft picks, and Dach is expected to debut between Michael Brandsegg-Nygård and J.T. Compher. Source: [dailyhive.com](https://dailyhive.com/vancouver/how-to-watch-streaming-only-canucks-red-wings-game) Source: [insidetherink.com](https://insidetherink.com/nhl-game-preview-vancouver-canucks-at-detroit-red-wings-with-line-combinations-11-25-2026/) Source: [nhl.com](https://www.nhl.com/canucks/news/game-notes-canucks-at-red-wings-112526) Source: [theprovince.com](https://theprovince.com/sports/hockey/nhl/vancouver-canucks/canucks-vs-red-wings-game-day-good-could-erase-one-bad-memory)

**B.C. Lions to hold training camp in Langford for next three seasons: Times Colonist**
The B.C. Lions will hold training camp in Langford for the next three seasons, the Times Colonist reports. Source: [timescolonist.com](https://www.timescolonist.com/sports/bc-lions-to-hold-training-camp-in-langford-for-next-three-seasons-13054964)

### Both Sides: Absorbing Surrey's development company
Surrey council is deciding whether the city-owned Surrey City Development Corp. stays an arm's-length builder or is absorbed into city hall. The company was created in 2007, with the city as sole shareholder, to develop surplus land. Mayor Doug McCallum dissolved it in 2020. Former mayor Brenda Locke revived it in late 2022. By 2023 it was working on a former Safeway site across from city hall — Locke's promised 10,000-seat arena, luxury hotel, conference space, homes and retail — plus Centre Block beside Surrey Central station, including space for Simon Fraser University's medical school, the Cloverdale Fairgrounds redevelopment, two tower projects near Gateway station, and a high-density mixed-use site in Newton.

McCallum's case is that the move keeps a campaign promise. "This is one of our promises in the campaign to download the Surrey development corporation into city operations, so this is the actual start of it," he said Monday. Council voted this week to terminate four independent directors. As of Wednesday the board is three city employees: city manager Rob Costanzo, finance director Vipin Sachdeva, and chief capital programs officer Jeff Arason. His report says integration is relatively straightforward, but some projects need special handling because of existing partnerships and continuing obligations, and staff are identifying those. McCallum also promised in the campaign to cancel the arena, so whether that project continues is unresolved.

Coun. Harry Bains, the only councillor outside the mayor's majority, was the only vote against removing the directors, on Monday and at the Nov. 9 meeting where the first integration vote was held. His case is that absorption "risks losing flexibility, focus and approach that make it a valuable municipal development tool." He asked what happens to company staff and what severance would be. Engineering manager Scott Neuman said he would not discuss severance, citing privacy, and that the city is looking at chances to integrate staff where possible. Coun. Doug Elford declined to comment and deferred to the mayor. The dated step now on the record is Wednesday's reduced board, with staff still sorting project obligations. Source: [vancouversun.com](https://vancouversun.com/news/surrey-moves-to-bring-real-estate-development-company-back-into-city-operations)

# Vancouver Daily News
> **A three-million-dollar yearly bill lands on Vancouver for living-wage recertification.**

**What You Need to Know:** Vancouver’s recertification as a living-wage employer adds a three-million-dollar yearly cost, the bill COPE Coun. Devyani Singh set against fireworks or food on the table. A Port Hardy family says 48-year-old Courtney McCowan died outside an emergency department that closes at 5 p.m., and Island Health and BC Emergency Health Services are reviewing it. A New Westminster man has been charged with second-degree murder in the death of Lions Bay actor Stewart McLean.

### Top Stories
**City of Vancouver’s recertification as living wage employer adds $3M annual cost: Vancouver Is Awesome**
Vancouver’s recertification as a living-wage employer adds $3 million a year in cost. COPE Coun. Devyani Singh said, “We could do fireworks or have people have food on their table.” Source: [vancouverisawesome.com](https://www.vancouverisawesome.com/economy-law-politics/city-of-vancouvers-recertification-as-living-wage-employer-adds-3m-annual-cost-13051152)

**Woman dies outside Port Hardy Hospital: Surrey Now-Leader**
Courtney McCowan, 48, died outside Port Hardy Hospital on November 19, and her daughter, Hailey Schubert, says a friend brought her about 10 to 11 minutes after the emergency department’s daily 5 p.m. closing. Schubert told Surrey Now-Leader her mother arrived at 5:11 p.m., that staff would not let her friend in, and that a paramedic already in the parking lot started CPR while two more ambulances came; she said the hospital later refused a paramedic trying to bring her mother in, then allowed entry after an estimated 39 minutes, a timeline the paper noted is unconfirmed. The union for Ambulance Paramedics of B.C. told Global News a paramedic noticed McCowan about 10 minutes after the doors shut and that paramedics gave CPR for upwards of 45 minutes on the sidewalk; BC Emergency Health Services said she was transferred to hospital staff. Health Minister Ryan Peterson said Island Health and BC Emergency Health Services are investigating, that care providers and paramedics responded and gave emergency interventions, and that he will work so the review’s findings lead to more reliable emergency care. Island Health said people who arrive just after closing are assessed for immediate treatment or a transfer, and that emergency-trained physicians and nurses, along with paramedics, provided emergency treatment in this case. Schubert is calling for rural emergency departments to stay open 24 hours, and she said people in town fear that after 5 p.m. the next hospital is a 40-minute drive to Fort McNeill. Source: [surreynowleader.com](https://surreynowleader.com/2026/11/23/woman-dies-outside-port-hardy-hospital/) Source: [globalnews.ca](https://globalnews.ca/news/12162537/bc-woman-dies-outside-emergency-room-closes-daily/)

**Man charged with second-degree murder in killing of B.C. actor Stewart McLean: North Shore News**
Nathan Neima, 35, of New Westminster, was arrested Saturday and charged with second-degree murder in the death of actor Stewart McLean, 45. He appeared Monday in provincial court in North Vancouver, with another procedural appearance set for January 6. McLean, whose credits include “Virgin River,” “Murder in a Small Town,” “Arrow” and “Travelers,” was reported missing on May 18 after he was last seen at his home in Lions Bay; Squamish RCMP said the Integrated Homicide Investigation Team took over after officers found evidence he was killed, and his remains were found days later in the Lions Bay area. Cpl. Esther Tupper said investigators believe the death was targeted, that the men were not strangers, that how they knew each other will be evidence in court, and that Neima does not have a criminal record. Actor and coach Jeff Seymour, speaking from Los Angeles, called the charge a “big relief” and said he was pleased police had pursued the case; he said McLean “didn’t cross lines” and was not involved in shady dealings, and that friends in Vancouver had not heard of the accused. Agent Jennifer Lee of Lucas Talent Inc. said she had worked with McLean since 2014 and that he was “the most positive, kind, funny, chill” person you could know. Tupper thanked Lions Bay residents and people in the film community, and said she hoped the charge brings some measure of peace. Source: [nsnews.com](https://www.nsnews.com/national-news/man-charged-with-second-degree-murder-in-killing-of-bc-actor-stewart-mclean-13048841) Source: [cbc.ca](https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/british-columbia/b-c-actor-stewart-mclean-murder-charge-9.7432598?cmp=rss)

**B.C. crime news: Man arrested after random assaults in downtown Vancouver: Vancouver Sun**
Vancouver police said they arrested a man after random assaults near a hotel at Burrard and Helmcken around 12:45 p.m. Friday: one woman reported being shoved into a window and toward stairs, another reported a threatening gesture, a third said she was punched in the back, and a man said he was shoved and threatened. The man was arrested about two blocks away, near Howe and Davie, and has been released with conditions while the investigation continues. On Saturday around 8:40 p.m., police said, a woman at Pullman Porter Street and East 1st Avenue in Olympic Village allegedly groped a father and tried to pull away a stroller with his one-year-old inside; he stopped her, the baby was not harmed, and a 42-year-old was arrested within three minutes. Charges have not been approved. Witnesses can call the VPD non-emergency line at 604-717-3321. Separately, police arrested a man Monday morning near West King Edward and Willow during a search-warrant investigation into a September 22 incident at Granville and Nelson, where a projectile from a grey pickup shattered the rear windshield of a police SUV; there were no injuries in the arrest. Coquitlam RCMP are also looking for two teens, described as 13 to 19, after a man who confronted them about fireworks in the 2600-block of Kingsway Avenue in Port Coquitlam just before 11:30 p.m. on November 10 was assaulted and taken to hospital, Sgt. Adriana O’Malley said. Anyone with video from 10:45 to 11:45 p.m. that night can call Coquitlam RCMP at 604-945-1550. Source: [vancouversun.com](https://vancouversun.com/news/bc-crime-news-nov-23-2026)

### City & Province
**B.C. Greens, including Leader Emily Lowan, sworn in as legislators in Victoria: North Shore News**
Green Leader Emily Lowan and caucus colleague Jeremy Valeriote have been sworn in at the legislature in Victoria, and Lowan is the youngest woman ever to sit there. Lowan said the Greens see areas of agreement with Premier Lorne Doerkson’s government but will hold the Conservatives and their “corporate lobbyists” accountable. She said British Columbians “shouldn’t have to keep bracing for the next climate disaster” after the United Nations climate conference in Turkey ended without a deal, and that countries on the front lines “were right to reject the deal” because an agreement that “ignores the cause of the crisis isn’t a deal worth signing.” She said the new Conservative government is moving in the wrong direction by promising to double natural gas production and triple liquefied natural gas exports. Global News reported New Democrats are to be sworn in Thursday morning. Source: [nsnews.com](https://www.nsnews.com/local-news/bc-greens-including-leader-emily-lowan-sworn-in-as-legislators-in-victoria-13047286) Source: [globalnews.ca](https://globalnews.ca/news/12162169/b-c-greens-oath-of-office/) Source: [theprogress.com](https://theprogress.com/2026/11/23/b-c-greens-lowan-becomes-youngest-woman-ever-in-b-c-legislature/)

**B.C. doctors urge Conservatives to make good on rural health promises: Vancouver Sun**
The B.C. College of Family Physicians is asking the new Conservative government to spend more on rural health care and to fulfill its promise to keep emergency rooms open. Among the asks from doctors and nurses is more opportunity for health-care training in small towns. Source: [vancouversun.com](https://vancouversun.com/news/bc-doctors-urge-conservatives-to-make-good-on-rural-health-promises)

**East Vancouver park identified for potential new community centre with 50-metre pool and two ice rinks: Daily Hive Vancouver**
Park Board staff, in a report for the November 30 meeting, identified the north playing fields at Kensington Park as the better East Vancouver site for a new community centre with a 50-metre pool and an ice rink, ahead of a simpler replacement at Hastings Community Park. The Kensington idea is still preliminary, with major construction funding likely left to capital plans beyond 2030; building on the field north of the 1980 centre would let people keep using that centre and its 15-metre pool, which has no lap lanes, during construction. A first rink could come in a later phase, the old buildings would then be demolished for replacement green space, and a second rink could follow on that footprint. The park sits between Knight Street, East 33rd Avenue, Dumfries Street and East 37th Avenue. Staff recommend seeking 2027 capital-budget money to design a replacement for Hastings Community Centre, parts of which date to 1936 and which ranked third for renewal in the 2022 strategy, behind Kensington; new buildings there would have to sit back from Renfrew Creek. The city’s 2027–2030 capital plan sets aside $496 million for recreation facilities. A 2025 Auditor General report found 72 per cent of Vancouver’s community and recreation facilities were in poor or very poor condition in 2022. The Downtown Vancouver Aquatic Centre, one of two city 50-metre pools along with Hillcrest, closed this past summer for redevelopment as a 25-metre, eight-lane pool, and demolition resumed this month after a Court of Appeal injunction expired. Last week the board opened the $91-million Marpole Community Centre, its first new community centre in 14 years, and this November 30 meeting is the first held at Vancouver City Hall under a pilot, instead of the Stanley Park headquarters. Source: [dailyhive.com](https://dailyhive.com/vancouver/kensington-park-hastings-community-park-new-facilities-pool-rink-vancouver)

### The Closer Look
**A private partner could be suitable to help achieve SFU Burnaby Mountain gondola, says TransLink CEO: Daily Hive Vancouver**
Design work on TransLink’s gondola from SkyTrain’s Production Way-University Station to Simon Fraser University’s Burnaby Mountain campus is about 50 per cent complete. Chief executive Kevin Quinn told the Greater Vancouver Board of Trade on November 20 that a private partner could help get it built, and that TransLink still needs the provincial and federal governments to help pay for construction and to keep the service running. He said he wants to work with SFU and both governments to secure that funding.

The heavy-duty line would run straight for 2.7 kilometres and climb about 370 metres, using cabins of about 30 passengers, similar to Whistler Blackcomb’s Peak to Peak. Peak capacity would be 3,000 passengers an hour each way, about 66 per cent higher than the 99 B-Line, with possible frequencies below a minute and a seven-minute end-to-end trip. Earlier renderings showed a large indoor concourse at the base as a transfer hall with the SkyTrain station. Opening the gondola would change the mountain bus network, especially by discontinuing the No. 145 from Production Way-University. Quinn said the other gain is buses put back into service: “our bus depots are packed to the gills.”

In 2022, TransLink estimated construction at about $210 million and said the project could be built in about 18 months once funding, design, planning and procurement were done. It had aimed to begin construction in 2025 or 2026. Daily Hive reported that after years of inflation in labour, equipment and materials, that figure is now likely highly outdated, and that it does not include possible extra geotechnical and design costs identified since.

Asked whether a public-private partnership could help build more transit, Quinn said, “Sure, certainly, the gondola [and] some other projects could be good candidates for that type of a [public-private partnership] model.” He also said TransLink can already borrow at low rates by issuing bonds, which gives it less reason than some other authorities to seek private financing. Daily Hive noted that Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government has been encouraging private investment in capital projects.

Quinn pointed to Surrey as proof that elections can change transit plans. On November 9, Mayor Doug McCallum and the new Safe Surrey Coalition council unanimously approved pursuing an Expo Line extension along King George Boulevard from Surrey City Centre to Newton Town Centre, now a key city priority. The previous council approved the King George Boulevard bus rapid transit line in May 2026; that line, between Surrey City Centre and Semiahmoo Town Centre via Newton, is expected to cost about $700 million, and Daily Hive reported it is unclear what would happen to it. Premier Lorne Doerkson has promised to build the Newton SkyTrain extension and, after he and his cabinet were sworn in, said it was a commitment, not merely a proposal. He cited that pursuit as one reason he chose Surrey-Newton MLA Harj Dhaliwal as parliamentary secretary for TransLink. Quinn said the Mayors’ Council decides which projects take priority. The council held its first meeting of the new term last week and reappointed Port Coquitlam Mayor Brad West as chair; 14 of the 21 mayors are newly elected. Quinn expects the new councils in Maple Ridge and the Township of Langley to reaffirm support soon for a proposed 22-kilometre Langley-Haney Place bus rapid transit line across the Golden Ears Bridge, linking Haney Place with the future Willowbrook Station on the Surrey-Langley extension.

Asked whether a Millennium Line extension from the new Arbutus Station to UBC could advance in the next several years, Quinn directed the question to the new provincial government. Extending the line west from Arbutus remains a priority in the Mayors’ Council plan through 2035, but the province is leading the detailed technical design, planning and business case. The previous BC NDP administration completed a significant portion of that technical work and business case. Quinn called the UBC extension “very complex” and “very expensive.” Source: [dailyhive.com](https://dailyhive.com/vancouver/translink-sfu-burnaby-mountain-gondola-capital-projects-update-november-2026)

### Also Today
**Who created Richmond's historic Hong Wo store? Volunteer unearths family's little-known role: CBC British Columbia**
A volunteer has found that a second family helped build and run Steveston’s Hong Wo store, opened in 1895 as Richmond’s first superstore, after decades in which records credited only Lam Ching Ling as proprietor. Source: [cbc.ca](https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/british-columbia/hong-wo-steveston-richmond-history-rewrite-9.7429092?cmp=rss)

**This B.C. man found some historical parkas at a thrift store — now he's trying to get them back to Nunavut: CBC British Columbia**
Mike Williams of Kamloops is trying to return thrift-store parkas made in Taloyoak, Nunavut, for the 1974 Arctic Winter Games in Alaska, to the community that made them. Source: [cbc.ca](https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/north/this-b-c-man-found-some-historical-parkas-at-a-thrift-store-now-he-s-trying-to-get-them-back-to-nunavut-9.7429862?cmp=rss)

**Delta’s new Chisholm Street Wharf now open: Surrey Now-Leader**
Delta’s new Chisholm Street Wharf is now open. Source: [surreynowleader.com](https://surreynowleader.com/2026/11/23/deltas-new-chisholm-street-wharf-now-open/)

### Both Sides: Who must be consulted on the KSM mine
The B.C. Supreme Court has ordered the province to reconsider a 2024 ruling that the Seabridge Gold KSM project had substantially started, and to consult the Tsetsaut Skii km Lax Ha Nation. Global News describes KSM, in the Golden Triangle, as one of the world’s largest undeveloped gold reserves and says it would be Canada’s largest gold mine if it proceeds.

The case for that consultation, as put by Ryan Beaton of Power Law for the TSKLH Nation and Chief Darlene Simpson, is that the province already had evidence the proposed waste-facility area is TSKLH territory. He said a 2023 assessment found that all evidence suggested that, and that the court agreed the province disregarded its own conclusions, which amounted to a failure to consult adequately. The nation says it is not opposed to the project. Beaton said members work in mining, that a strong economy and good projects matter to them as to other British Columbians, and that they want this one done efficiently, responsibly and sustainably, with their rights honoured.

The case against treating TSKLH as a rights holder there comes from the Nisga’a Nation and the Tahltan Nation, who support the project and the substantial-start decision. They said they are the rights holders and decision makers for their territories, that they do not recognize TSKLH as holding any Aboriginal rights or title there, and that they reject TSKLH claims on KSM, which they say is in Tahltan territory and in the Nass Area and Nass Wildlife Area under the Nisga’a Final Agreement. They called such claims “opportunistic and unsupported,” and said B.C.’s wider consultation approach has increased claims by groups with unsupported, marginal or speculative claims, creating uncertainty and disrespecting treaty rights and proper rights and title holders. They said they are concerned that approach empowers groups who do not hold rights-holders’ obligations to hijack and derail project reviews.

The designation now goes back for reconsideration and consultation with TSKLH. The B.C. Mining Association estimates Golden Triangle projects will generate nearly $800 billion in economic activity over the next two decades. Source: [globalnews.ca](https://globalnews.ca/news/12162930/court-setback-major-mining-project-bc-golden-triangle/)

# Vancouver Daily News
> **748 non-market homes go to a Surrey public hearing Monday night.**

**What You Need to Know:** Surrey council takes up a plan for 748 non-market homes in two City Centre towers after a public hearing Monday night. An 84-year-old woman was killed in a Burnaby collision Saturday, and a First Nations leader warned of dire consequences if the province repeals its Indigenous rights law. A coroner's jury has issued recommendations after police shot and killed an autistic Surrey teen in 2025.

### Top Stories
**Hundreds of non-market housing units in two towers proposed for Surrey City Centre: Vancouver Sun**
Two proposed high-rises in Surrey's City Centre would replace the aging Jessica Place townhouse complex at 9883 140 Street, a short walk from the Green Timbers SkyTrain station under construction at 140 Street and Fraser Highway. Ron Gill, Surrey's general manager of planning and development, said the existing buildings hold 40 below-market rental units and that all of those residents will be offered the chance to move into the new buildings once they are built on the site. Gill said staff support the plan because it would add mixed-income affordable rental housing in City Centre and higher density near frequent transit. The first tower would be 35 storeys with 327 units and the second 39 storeys with 421 units, 748 in all, kept non-market for 60 years. Surrey council votes after a public hearing Monday night. Gill said a reputable non-profit would operate the homes at rent-geared-to-income or low-end-of-market rates. Entre Nous Femmes Housing Society says it first applied in June 2025, expects construction to start in summer 2027, expects that work to last three years, and projects an opening in summer 2030. The society says existing residents will have to relocate temporarily because every current building would be demolished. The plan includes a management office and two ground-oriented, daycare-ready townhouse units that could run child care as a home occupation. The 35-storey tower would have indoor and outdoor amenities, a community garden, meeting rooms, a gymnasium and a co-working area; the 39-storey tower would have a community garden, amenities, an outdoor playground, seating, a basketball court and a stage. Shared private amenities are proposed for both buildings. The school district estimates 62 school-age children. Source: [vancouversun.com](https://vancouversun.com/business/real-estate/hundreds-of-non-market-housing-units-in-two-towers-proposed-for-surrey-city-centre)

**Woman struck and killed by vehicle in Burnaby: Vancouver Sun**
An 84-year-old woman was struck by a vehicle and killed in Burnaby on Saturday night. Burnaby RCMP Cpl. Mike Kalanj said it happened around 7:20 p.m. on Kingsway at Randolph Avenue. Kalanj said she was declared dead at the scene and the driver remained and is co-operating with the investigation. The Vancouver Sun notes two earlier deaths of elderly women on foot in Vancouver this month. On Nov. 6, a 78-year-old woman was struck while crossing Dunbar Street at West 34th Avenue; that driver stopped and co-operated, and she died the next day. On Nov. 11, an 87-year-old woman was crossing Dunbar Street at West 41st Avenue in a marked crosswalk when a white sedan turning off West 41st onto Dunbar struck her; she died on Nov. 17, and police have not located that driver. Source: [vancouversun.com](https://vancouversun.com/news/elderly-woman-struck-and-killed-by-vehicle-in-burnaby) Source: [cbc.ca](https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/british-columbia/burnaby-fatal-collision-84-year-old-woman-9.7431971?cmp=rss)

**First Nations leader warns of consequences if B.C. repeals DRIPA: CBC British Columbia**

Source: [cbc.ca](https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/british-columbia/first-nations-leader-warns-consequences-of-dripa-repeal-9.7432127?cmp=rss)

**Tumbler Ridge begins consultation on design for new school building: Global BC**
Residents of Tumbler Ridge are being asked for feedback on designs for a new secondary school after a mass shooting there in February. Global BC reports six people were killed when 18-year-old Jesse Van Rootselaar opened fire at the northeastern B.C. school on Feb. 10; before that, she killed her mother and half-brother at their home, and she died at the school from a self-inflicted gunshot. In July, School District 59 began demolition after then-Premier David Eby said students cannot return to the school where the shootings happened. Board chair Chad Anderson said the board has narrowed the choices to a pre-fabricated building, largely built off-site and assembled on site, and a site-built design, and hopes the result is a place where students and staff feel safe. A two-week survey of residents will feed a board decision expected by late this winter. Anderson said that if all goes well, construction could begin in summer 2027, depending on the method chosen. Source: [globalnews.ca](https://globalnews.ca/news/12161632/tumbler-ridge-new-school-building/)

### The Closer Look
**Coroner's jury makes recommendations in police shooting of autistic Surrey teen: Vancouver Sun**
A B.C. coroner's jury has recommended that police and health agencies co-ordinate emergency responses more closely after 15-year-old Chase de Balinhard was shot and killed by police in Surrey. He died on Feb. 9, 2025, after a 911 call about a teen with a gun led to a standoff of nearly half an hour. The gun was fake. Officers did not know that. After he ignored repeated requests to drop it, he was fatally shot in the chest. An officer who testified during an emotional week in Burnaby coroners' court said police knew Chase was neurodivergent but had not received specific training on how to de-escalate a situation like that one.

The jury asked the Ministry of Public Safety, the Ministry of Health and the Fraser Health Authority to review how crisis and safety information can be easier to reach in an emergency. That would include voluntarily provided health records and personalized safety plans, such as safe words or calming techniques, for responders. Health officials are urged to make individualized safety plans easier to find and to review and update them regularly. Those plans could tell responders whether a youth's home contains low-velocity, imitation or conventional firearms.

Vancouver Coastal Health, Fraser Health, the RCMP and Surrey Police Service are asked to consider whether police and mental-health response teams have enough capacity and equipment, and whether mobile integrated crisis response teams — formerly known as Car 67 in Fraser Health — need more resources and a wider geographical range. The Ministry of Health is asked to review whether psychiatric nurses attached to police mental-health teams can get time-sensitive health information, including someone's individualized safety plan, in a crisis.

At the federal and provincial level, the jury asked whether realistic imitation firearms and pellet guns can be made easier to identify with a clear, conspicuous visual cue that they are fake or low-velocity, including product, manufacturing and import rules so those markers cannot be removed or altered, and whether the Firearm Violence Prevention Act should add provisions on imitation guns. The Ministry of Education and Child Care and the Ministry of Children and Family Development are asked to review how supports for children with autism or other neurodivergence are delivered and monitored, including how changes to those supports are communicated to families.

The Independent Investigations Office of B.C. is asked to review how family members get information during an investigation into a police-involved incident, including whether families get clear and timely information about what can be shared, what cannot yet be shared, and why, and whether that process can meet or exceed police-based victim services. Police in Surrey are urged to review how they contact family if a first attempt fails, including whether that should follow a set protocol or stay with the officers' discretion; to review whether Surrey Police Service has adequate access to helicopters and drones in an emergency; and to explore ways to improve trust between youth and police in Surrey schools. Health and school officials are asked to determine whether families of autistic and neurodivergent children and youth in Surrey have clear information about existing autism and mental-health supports and how to access them. A coroner's jury establishes the facts around a death and can make recommendations. It does not assign blame and cannot call for a criminal investigation. Source: [vancouversun.com](https://vancouversun.com/news/coroners-jury-makes-recommendations-in-police-shooting-of-autistic-surrey-teen)

### Getting Around

Highway 1 is closed from 256th Street in the Township of Langley to Lefeuvre Road in Abbotsford until 12 a.m. on Dec. 31, with a detour and eastbound traffic shifted south of the median. Separate night construction on Highway 1 runs until Dec. 15, with a 60 km/h speed limit and single-lane traffic in both directions, from 9 p.m. to 5:30 a.m. on weeknights and 9 p.m. to 7:30 a.m. on weekends. Bridge construction on Highway 7B in Port Coquitlam, between United Boulevard and Shaughnessy Street, continues weekdays from 7 a.m. to 5 p.m., with two lanes each way, width restrictions, a rule that commercial vehicles use both lanes, and a permit required for oversized loads; the Queensborough Bridge on Highway 91A in New Westminster is reduced to one lane each direction on its overnight maintenance windows. No watches or warnings are in effect for Vancouver. It is cloudy and 6.4 degrees now. Monday brings periods of rain, about 5 millimetres, an east wind of 20 km/h gusting to 40, and a high of 9; Monday night turns to rain of 15 to 25 millimetres with the same wind and a low of 7; Tuesday is rainy, still windy from the east at 20 gusting to 40, with a high of 12. Source: [drivebc.ca](https://www.drivebc.ca/) Source: [weather.gc.ca](https://weather.gc.ca/rss/weather/49.245_-123.115_e.xml)

### Sports
**Blackhawks rookie Roman Kantserov scores first NHL hat trick in win over Canucks: Toronto Star**
The Chicago Blackhawks beat the Vancouver Canucks 6-3 at Rogers Arena. Rookie Roman Kantserov scored his first NHL hat trick, including the goal that ended Vancouver's comeback hopes. Chicago led 4-0 before Vancouver managed a shot; the first Canucks shot came 13 minutes in, and the crowd answered with a Bronx cheer. Frank Nazar, Tyler Bertuzzi, Kantserov and Dominic Toninato scored in that opening burst. Nikita Tolopilo was pulled after the fourth goal. Kevin Lankinen, in net for the first time since Nov. 3, stopped 17 of 19 shots. Head coach Manny Malhotra said Tolopilo was put in a bad situation, that the group in front of him was not ready, and that Lankinen did a good job after being thrown into a rough spot. Vancouver's goals came from a Zeev Buium point shot that Kevin Korchinski tipped into his own net, a Filip Chytil pass that banked in off Jordan Greenway, and a Jake DeBrusk rebound. Brock Boeser's assist on the DeBrusk goal extended his point streak to 11 games, tied for the 17th-longest in Canucks history; the club record is 15, shared by Petr Nedved and Todd Bertuzzi. Vancouver's power play was 0-for-5. Chicago's was 3-for-4 and moved from 27th in the league to 16th. Vancouver's penalty kill sits at 61.2 per cent, just ahead of Seattle's 60.7 per cent. The win moved Chicago out of second-last and into 29th, ahead of the Los Angeles Kings and the Pittsburgh Penguins. Chytil said the team did not help Tolopilo and that he was not happy with his own game. Boeser said an unlucky bounce after a good first shift cannot be allowed to deflate the team. Source: [thestar.com](https://www.thestar.com/sports/hockey/blackhawks-rookie-roman-kantserov-scores-first-nhl-hat-trick-in-win-over-canucks/article_d860f36d-a13c-55da-af69-8a98fe562146.html) Source: [dailyhive.com](https://dailyhive.com/vancouver/i-watched-this-game-canucks-blackhawks-landon-dupont-sweepstakes) Source: [thehockeynews.com](https://thehockeynews.com/nhl/vancouver-canucks/game-day/3-standouts-from-game-26-blackhawks-6-canucks-3)

> **Sixty thousand B.C. nurses get three percent a year, not the eight they sought.**

Sunshine Coast RCMP say they have identified the driver and located the truck and trailer in the Sechelt hit-and-run that killed a 16-year-old earlier this week.

### Top Stories
**B.C. nurses union 'gravely disappointed' with 3% wage hike in arbitrated settlement: CBC British Columbia**
Arbitrators have imposed annual wage increases of three percent through 2029 for British Columbia’s more than 60,000 nurses. The B.C. Nurses’ Union had asked for eight percent a year. ### The Closer Look
**B.C. moves to seize cars, cash, Rolexes and drug lab properties in the Fraser Valley: Vancouver Sun**
B.C.’s director of civil forfeiture has filed in B.C. Supreme Court against 10 owners and their companies, seeking forfeiture of five Fraser Valley properties police allege were used to make and sell drugs through a drug superlab. The lawsuit also seeks a 2024 Jeep Cherokee, a 2017 Dodge Ram, a 2019 Audi A7, and jewelry including two Rolex watches, two Cartier bracelets and a Van Cleef and Arpels bracelet. Police seized cash they say came from illegal activities in 10 listed amounts from $89 to $15,550, about $38,000 in total. None of the allegations has been proven in court.

The searches of properties and vehicles were on Oct. 2, 2025, a day after undercover RCMP officers watched two men transport containers of chemicals to a clandestine lab on South Sumas Road in Chilliwack, according to the lawsuit. Those warrants followed two police operations in 2025 and 2026 aimed at labs producing fentanyl, methamphetamine, MDMA and other street drugs. At the South Sumas property, police found chemicals, equipment and recipes, including 39 kilograms of fentanyl and 3,766 MDMA pills. The Vancouver Sun reports that police seized more fentanyl at that Chilliwack lab than in the previous Canadian record bust in Falkland. Cellphones showed extensive communications between Justin Fauth and Carlos Martinez about drug production and trafficking, the lawsuit says. That investigation led police to Nigel Kiyoshi Yakashiro; the filing says he had no source of lawful income and was highly surveillance conscious.

Fauth and Martinez face criminal drug charges. They are among 10 individuals and two companies, plus the bankruptcy trustee for the estate of an 11th person, named as owners of property the province intends to keep as the means or proceeds of crime. Also named are Yakashiro, Ravinder (Robbie) Singh Ghag, Dharminder (Happy) Singh Ghag, Swarn Singh Ghag, Courtney MacKenzie, Roopwant Badwal, Alexis Coughlan, Carley Kristine Tower, the estate of Satnam (Sonny) Singh Ghag, SGASS Holding Co. and Ghag & Ghag Co. The lawsuit alleges the defendants manufactured, possessed and trafficked drugs and disposed of hazardous wastes, and that Fauth, Martinez and Yakashiro were members of a group whose main purposes included drug production and trafficking for financial benefit.

Three properties were connected to the Ghag family, including South Sumas Road, and two were leased to Fauth and Martinez, who the lawsuit says conducted secret meetings and ran a lab there and used a third Ghag property for chemical disposal. The filing alleges the Ghags knew or were wilfully blind to that use. Martinez lived with Badwal at a fourth property on Sheffield Way in Chilliwack, which Badwal owned and where police allegedly found fentanyl, trafficking equipment and about $13,000 in cash. Yakashiro and Tower owned a fifth property, in Abbotsford, where the lawsuit says cash and jewelry seized on July 9 were proceeds of crime and Yakashiro’s Jeep Cherokee was used for trafficking. The lawsuit also says Fauth and MacKenzie rented a house in Lindell Beach where police found fentanyl and MDMA, trafficking equipment and records, fake ID, about $16,000 in cash and the two Rolexes. Source: [vancouversun.com](https://vancouversun.com/news/bc-moves-to-seize-cars-cash-rolexes-and-drug-lab-properties-in-the-fraser-valley)

### Getting Around
Highway 7B in Port Coquitlam, between United Boulevard and Shaughnessy Street, has one lane closed each way from 8 p.m. Nov. 21 until 9 a.m. today, with weekday bridge construction, congestion delays, width restrictions, a requirement that commercial vehicles use both lanes, and permits for oversized loads. Highway 7 in Maple Ridge, 67 metres east of 240 Street, has lane closures both ways and a 24/7 median crossover until 5 a.m. Friday, Nov. 27, with both directions down to one lane, westbound traffic directed into an eastbound lane, and both westbound lanes fully closed. Highway 1 from 256th Street in Langley to Lefeuvre Road in Abbotsford is closed all day, every day, until Dec. 31, with a detour and eastbound traffic shifted south of the median. Highway 91A’s Queensborough Bridge in New Westminster is reduced to one lane each way for overnight maintenance, and separate Highway 1 night construction through Dec. 15 limits speed to 60 km/h with single-lane traffic both ways. # Vancouver Daily News
> **A one-thousand-dollar B.C. tax cut now waits for a spring twenty twenty-seven bill.**

**What You Need to Know:** Premier Lorne Doerkson says the promised one-thousand-dollar B.C. income tax cut will reach the legislature in spring 2027, and he hopes, without promising the date, that it will be dated to January 1. Investigators have named the two people killed outside a Surrey Walmart on November 15. Canada's first climate lawsuit to reach trial has wrapped witness testimony in Federal Court in Vancouver.

### Top Stories
**Premier Lorne Doerkson signals $1,000 B.C. income tax cut in Spring 2027: Daily Hive Vancouver**
Premier Lorne Doerkson says his newly sworn-in Conservative government will bring its promised $1,000 annual provincial income tax cut to the legislature in the spring 2027 session. He told reporters today, just after he and his cabinet were sworn in at Government House, "We're committed to doing that, and it will happen in certainly the spring session. My hope, don't hold me to this, my hope is that that will be dated back to Jan. 1." A fall sitting was ruled out this week. The Conservative platform would raise the basic personal amount from $13,216 to $32,000. The party estimated about $1,000 a year for someone who would otherwise pay at least that much in B.C. income tax, or about $2,000 for a couple if both qualify, and a smaller saving or none for someone who already pays little or no provincial income tax. The platform put the cost at $725 million before March 31, 2027, and $2.9 billion for each full year after. The former BC NDP September forecast put the 2026/2027 deficit at $13.8 billion; the Conservatives' own plan still projected $13.7 billion that year. Finance Minister Peter Milobar, sworn in today, accused former premier David Eby during the October 2026 campaign of breaking a grocery-rebate promise the NDP administration shelved in February 2025. Doerkson also named Carson Binda, formerly the B.C. director of the Canadian Taxpayers Federation, Minister of State for Red Tape Reduction, and first-time Coquitlam-Burke Mountain MLA Ryan Peterson as health minister, citing a ministry the previous government budgeted at $40.6 billion for 2026/2027. Source: [dailyhive.com](https://dailyhive.com/vancouver/lorne-doerkson-bc-income-tax-cut-promise-spring-2027)

**Police identify victims of fatal double shooting at Surrey Walmart parking lot: Philippine Canadian Inquirer**
The Integrated Homicide Investigation Team has identified the two people killed in a shooting outside a Walmart in Surrey as 23-year-old Gaganpreet "Garry" Rehal and 24-year-old Sukhjeet Kaur, both of Delta. Surrey Police Service officers and paramedics answered reports of gunfire in a parking lot near 88 Avenue and 124 Street at about 10:38 p.m. on November 15. Both were found with gunshot wounds and later pronounced dead in hospital. Police later found a burned four-door sedan in the 9700 block of Princess Drive that investigators believe is connected, and they are trying to identify occupants who fled. IHIT said Rehal had previous police interactions involving weapons and firearms-related offences, that Kaur had limited known contacts with authorities in Canada, and that investigators believe the shooting was targeted and showed indicators of organized crime. Spokesperson Sgt. Freda Fong said investigators are working with the families on the victims' movements before the shooting. Police want witnesses, surveillance and dashcam from the shooting scene and the vehicle fire between 10 p.m. and 11 p.m. on November 15, at 1-877-551-4448. Source: [canadianinquirer.net](https://canadianinquirer.net/2026/11/21/police-identify-victims-of-fatal-double-shooting-at-surrey-walmart-parking-lot/) Source: [telegraphindia.com](https://www.telegraphindia.com/world/canada-police-identify-two-indian-origin-victims-of-fatal-shooting-outside-surrey-walmart/cid/2190618)

**Canada's first climate lawsuit to go to trial has wrapped up hearings: CBC British Columbia**

**Crucifix erected on White Rock breakwater ‘not appropriate’: Surrey Now-Leader**

A visitor who asked not to be named told Surrey Now-Leader she and her husband saw it on November 19, estimated it at about four feet, and called it engineered rather than a couple of boards; it bears the inscription John 14:6. She said staff told her many complaints were already in and that a marine contractor would remove it sometime in December, and she is annoyed taxpayer money has to pay for that. The City of White Rock said the Parks Bylaw does not allow structures or other items on the breakwater, and that its marine contractor will remove the items in the next few weeks as scheduling permits. ### The Closer Look
**Adopt-A-School: 'Halting Hunger' a priority for students facing challenges: Vancouver Sun**
Learning Pathways, an alternative program for 18 students in Burnaby, is asking The Vancouver Sun's Adopt-A-School program for a $6,500 grant for breakfast, lunch and snacks. Youth engagement worker Adèle Cooshek added a line that matches the request's name, Halting Hunger: "Without food, our classes fall apart." The meals would be at the Canada Way Learning Centre, 5310 Woodsworth Street.

Cooshek said a number of the students have learning issues or mental health challenges, and some are dealing with trauma, family instability, financial hardship, and a lack of guaranteed access to food. She said Halting Hunger addresses food insecurity among vulnerable youth in the alternative secondary program. The students do not function well in a regular school, she said. Some will transition back. They can also complete a Dogwood diploma, the Grade 12 graduation certificate, through the program. That takes regular attendance, and she said being able to feed students is key to them showing up.

Adopt-A-School first helped the program last year. Cooshek called it magnificent and said attendance improved dramatically. She said a number of the kids come to school hungry, without breakfast, and then go through a great deal of food. She wants them to eat so they can self-regulate and focus on academics and the other things the program offers.

Other organizations are already involved. The Take A Hike Foundation provides a once-a-week trip outdoors. The Cinderella Project helps disadvantaged youth prepare for graduation, supplying attire, hair care, makeup, portraits and mentorship. Cooshek said one student graduating this year was enrolled in that project. That student's goal is to help people facing homelessness. She wants post-secondary courses after graduation so she can do that work, though she might not be able to afford them right away. Cooshek said the student has already taken in a classmate who does not have a home to go to.

Adopt-A-School has sent more than $17.5 million to hundreds of schools in B.C. since 2011 to feed and clothe children, setting up breakfast and lunch programs at schools' request. This year more than 300 schools are seeking $2.6 million, the largest number of requests ever, for thousands of children lacking food, clothing and other necessities. It is a registered charity administered by The Vancouver Sun Children's Fund board. No administration fees are taken from donations. The paper says 100 percent of the money is directed to schools. Donations can be made at vansunkidsfund.ca or by credit card at 236-998-7570. # Vancouver Daily News
> **One hundred twenty million dollars in Vancouver budget cuts now face a public audit.**

**What You Need to Know:** Vancouver's new council has ordered a public accounting of one hundred twenty million dollars in 2026 budget cuts, with a staff report due in the first quarter of 2027. Only Councillor Mike Klassen voted against the audit and a companion motion on city policy. The same meeting delayed a gas water-heater ban to 2028 and cancelled a sidewalk robot-delivery pilot.

### Top Stories
**Vancouver Council Passes ‘the People’s Audit’: The Tyee**
At its second meeting, the newly elected council authorized a People's Audit of the 2026 budget cuts and passed an omnibus motion titled Restoring Vancouver's Leadership as an Inclusive, Compassionate and Resilient City. Only Councillor Mike Klassen voted no. COPE Councillor Sean Orr's audit requires staff to report in public in the first quarter of 2027 on the effects of $120 million in cuts, including job eliminations, vacancies, layoffs, cancelled projects and reduced hours back to January 1, 2024. Council also directed staff to carry out a June report on ending traffic deaths and injuries, including recommendations for 30 or 40 km/h limits on major streets, after three pedestrians were killed and two injured since late October, among them an 87-year-old woman whose death Vancouver police announced in November. It put off a gas water-heater ban until January 1, 2028: the BC Coalition for Affordable Dependable Energy argued for consumer choice and affordability, and said a municipal ban clashed with provincial promises to undo such limits, while speakers from the Canadian National Institute for the Blind argued electrification protects health and the environment. Council cancelled a robot food-delivery pilot that Serve Robotics' Vignesh Ram defended as an evidence trial for which the city had already hired local staff; the Canadian National Institute for the Blind and Vision Zero Vancouver said the machines threaten people who need clear, predictable sidewalks. Source: [thetyee.ca](https://thetyee.ca/News/2026/11/20/Vancouver-Council-Passes-Peoples-Audit/) Source: [english.pravda.ru](https://english.pravda.ru/news/world/173703-vancouver-council-budget-audit-policy-reversal/)

**British Columbia’s premier-designate Lorne Doerkson, cabinet to be sworn in: Global BC**
Lorne Doerkson is to be sworn in today at Government House as British Columbia's 38th premier, with his ministers, and to unveil a first cabinet — a day after Conservative MLAs took their oaths, and as the first Conservative government in almost a century takes office. Peter Milobar, the party's former finance critic, says Doerkson has an embarrassment of riches in skills on the elected team and a place for everyone to contribute. Caroline Elliott, who narrowly lost the leadership to former leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay, says she does not know what role she will have and will be glad to represent her constituents. UBC political science lecturer Stewart Prest expects a relatively smaller cabinet than under John Horgan and David Eby, and describes the choices as a multi-dimensional balancing act across regions and the population. Elections BC's official count is 64 Conservatives, 27 NDP members and two Greens, with judicial recounts in two ridings won by fewer than 50 votes, one by a Conservative and one by a New Democrat. Source: [globalnews.ca](https://globalnews.ca/news/12159369/lorne-doerkson-swearing-in/) Source: [dailyhive.com](https://dailyhive.com/vancouver/lorne-doerkson-bc-conservative-mlas-sworn-in-oaths-november-2026)

# Vancouver Daily News
> **Workers in Metro Vancouver now need $28.55 an hour to cover essential costs.**

**What You Need to Know:** Workers in Metro Vancouver now need $28.55 an hour to cover essential costs, BC Policy Solutions says in its 2026 living-wage report, up from $27.85 last year and $10.30 above the provincial minimum. Vancouver council has ordered funding for 100 new bus shelters by September 2027. An 87-year-old woman struck in a Dunbar crosswalk on Remembrance Day has died, and police are still looking for the driver.

### Top Stories
**Metro Vancouver's living wage has increased as everyday costs rise: Daily Hive**
BC Policy Solutions, in its BC Living Wage 2026 report, calculates the hourly wage a full-time worker needs to cover essential expenses, avoid chronic financial stress, and take part in community life. In Metro Vancouver that figure is $28.55, a 2.5 per cent rise from 2025’s $27.85, and $10.30 above B.C.’s $18.25 minimum wage. The institute’s press release says the increase reflects wages not keeping up with the cost of living; it ties higher prices for food, fuel, clothing and footwear to the trade war with the U.S. and the war in Iran. It says 35 per cent of Metro Vancouver workers, more than half a million people, earn less than the living wage. Lead author Iglika Ivanova, co-executive director and senior economist, says the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation reports rent cuts and vacancies concentrated in new high-end buildings, while the market stays tight for lower-income households, especially families needing two or more bedrooms. Food, the second-largest expense in the living-wage budget, rose 4.1 per cent from last year, and out-of-pocket childcare for the living-wage family of four rose by nearly $160 a month. The report says the wage would have been higher without the Canadian Dental Care Plan, the Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit and the BC Rental Assistance Program, and that ending the BC Climate Action Tax Credit hurt low-wage earners without children. Co-author Navdeep Singh Chhina, managing director of Living Wage BC, called on the incoming provincial government to invest in affordable housing, public transit and childcare. Squamish’s living wage is $29.05, up 3.8 per cent, and Whistler’s is $30.50, up 3 per cent; the lowest in B.C. is Grand Forks at $22.15, and Port Alberni is $23.75. Source: [dailyhive.com](https://dailyhive.com/vancouver/metro-vancouver-living-wage-increases-2026) Source: [biv.com](https://www.biv.com/news/economy-law-politics/metro-vancouver-workers-need-2855hour-to-get-by-report-13031489)

**Elderly victim of Vancouver hit-and-run dies in hospital: Vancouver Sun**
An 87-year-old woman struck and seriously injured in Vancouver on Remembrance Day has died. Vancouver Police Department spokesperson Sgt. Adam Donaldson said she was crossing Dunbar Street at West 41st Avenue in a marked crosswalk when a white sedan turning off West 41st onto Dunbar hit her. She was taken to hospital and died on Tuesday, November 17. Donaldson said police are still searching for the driver and the vehicle, described as a two-door Mercedes C-Class, possibly white, grey or silver, with a model year between 2002 and 2005. Five days earlier, a 78-year-old woman was struck on Dunbar Street at West 34th Avenue in an unmarked crosswalk; that driver stopped and co-operated, and she died the next day. Source: [vancouversun.com](https://vancouversun.com/news/elderly-victim-of-vancouver-hit-and-run-dies-in-hospital)

### The Closer Look
**Vancouver City Council approves goal of 100 new TransLink bus shelters, aims to cover every stop where space allows by 2029: Daily Hive**
Vancouver City Council has unanimously approved a plan to add a shelter with seating at 100 TransLink bus stops that lack one, with those shelters to be installed by September 2027. The amended motion from COPE councillor Sean Orr passed at the November 18, 2026 public meeting, the same night council approved all 11 member motions on the agenda. Staff must put funding for the first 100 locations into the 2027 budget, generally the busier suitable stops without shelters, and report back by April 2027 on options to put a shelter and bench at every stop where it physically fits, by December 2029.

Orr presented it as access for people who depend on the bus. He said someone with a disability, or a senior with mobility trouble, should not have to stand in the rain to go about daily business, and he said the amenities help ridership. He credited COPE colleague Solomon Yi-Kieran with leading the drafting. They estimate only about half of Vancouver’s stops have a shelter with a bench. Expanding shelters was a COPE platform promise, and Yi-Kieran has called transit improvements a core priority. He said that as a rider he knows waiting half an hour in the rain for the No. 3, the No. 8 or the No. 49 with no bench or cover, and that with rain more than 40 per cent of the year, about half of stops without a covered bench is not acceptable.

TransLink handles shelters on its own property, such as off-street exchanges. On sidewalk stops, Metro Vancouver cities generally install and maintain them. Mayor Pete Fry sought a fuller account of the ongoing work and spending to keep shelters clean, safe, accessible and usable. Green councillor Stephanie Smith amended the motion so staff weigh weather exposure, safety and barriers to access, including for seniors and people with disabilities, not boarding totals alone. Some stops have no shelter because the sidewalk is narrow, the curb sits close to a property line, or trees and utilities are in the way. After suggestions from ABC councillor Mike Klassen, staff must determine how much money is available, what TransLink and others might contribute, and how much more is needed, including possible reallocation inside the 2027–2030 capital plan. Astral/JCDecaux is the long-term street-furniture contractor: it installs, operates and maintains shelters and receives the advertising revenue. Staff will consider designs, that revenue and possible changes to the partnership, plus solar-powered lighting, garbage bins and safety features. Designs have generally not changed since the early 2000s, when the city signed the first 20-year contract.

Denis Agar, executive director of the transit advocacy group Movement, told council that a long wait with no bench is part of the mobility gap between people who can drive and people who cannot, and that the gap can be fixed. Orr pointed to Burnaby, which launched an expansion in 2023 aimed at 370 new shelters by 2030, choosing sites by ridership and by proximity to schools, seniors centres and civic facilities. A 2021 Burnaby staff report estimated about $30,000 to design, fabricate and install each lighted shelter, a figure likely higher after later price rises. Burnaby then had 968 stops, 231 with a shelter and 737 with only a bench or nothing; at the 2021 unit cost, covering the rest was roughly $22 million before later inflation. New Westminster is replacing 50 shelters through Pattison Outdoor by the end of 2026, adding 14 in January 2027 for a municipal total of 64, with a longer aim of about 100. Source: [dailyhive.com](https://dailyhive.com/vancouver/vancouver-city-council-translink-bus-shelter-target-goal-approved)

**Behind the scenes of one of B.C.’s highest Christmas attractions: Vancouver Sun**
Canyon Lights at Capilano Suspension Bridge Park runs November 20 to January 10, except December 25, from 11 a.m. to 10 p.m., in its 20th year, with a new Light Storm installation in Cliffwalk Gardens. Tickets are $29.95 for children and $76.95 for adults at capbridge.com. Rope-access lead David Trautman said the tallest climbs are over 100 feet, Wildlight has moved onto bigger trees with an upgraded projector, and a three-person climbing crew has been installing since preparations shifted from Canyon Frights in early October. ### Both Sides: Hotel rooms and a Mount Pleasant rental
Yesterday’s new Vancouver council was already taking up reversals of the last term’s decisions. On Wednesday, November 18, COPE councillors Solomon Yi-Kieran and Chloe Leslie asked whether that reaches the Hotel Development Policy and a rezoning approved only in principle.

Michael Cook, chair of the Myron Manor Collective and a member of the Vancouver Tenants Union, asked the new council to repeal previously approved hotel bylaws and rezonings, especially his building, and send them back to staff. Myron Manor, at 75 East 8th Avenue, is a three-storey rental with more than two dozen units near the future Mount Pleasant SkyTrain station. On July 28, after a hearing over three dates, the previous council approved in principle a 21-storey tower with 190 hotel units and two storeys of industrial space, led by Lotus Capital Corporation and Nicola Real Estate. Cook’s stated reason is that rental homes should not be replaced by hotels. He asked council to repeal subsection 3.2.2.1(d) and replace it with a binding rule that no rental apartments in the city be replaced by hotels, and he proposed a municipal fund so tenant groups could buy buildings and convert them to co-operatives or community land trusts.

The policy, approved in April 2025 and last amended in May 2026, is the city’s tool for a net 10,000 hotel rooms over the coming decades. The City and Destination Vancouver say extra rooms are needed for tourism, jobs and major events. Destination Vancouver says the region, especially Vancouver, faces a room shortage visible in occupancy and overnight rates, and that the city’s hotel supply is lower than in the early 2000s even as short-term rentals were restricted. City staff have said Vancouver is on track against the room goal based on projects in the pipeline, while many remain proposals and approved projects may not be built. The policy also allows hotels mixed with rental or strata housing, which staff say has helped make new housing financially viable. Unite Here Local 40, which represents many hotel workers, has opposed several hotel proposals and policies and has launched court challenges; in July 2026 public hearings, then-ABC councillors accused the union and its supporters of filibuster tactics.

City staff told council that folding Cook’s requests into a tenant-rights motion would greatly expand the work, that repealing a rezoning is possible but “very complex,” and that council can also decline to enact a rezoning bylaw after an in-principle approval. They said they would brief council later on the policy and on subsection 3.2.2.1(d). A separate report on a 15-storey, 151-room hotel at 852-872 Seymour Street was withdrawn from the November 17 agenda; staff had urged a public hearing and then rejection because of impacts on adjacent towers. Source: [dailyhive.com](https://dailyhive.com/vancouver/vancouver-city-council-reverse-rezonings-hotel-policy-repeal-november-2026)
