# Vancouver Daily News
> **About one acre of Chinatown grass is now a permanent park, keeping a fire-hall plan off the site.**

**What You Need to Know:** Vancouver council has given permanent park status to about one acre at Gore and Union, land once held for a freeway ramp and later eyed for a temporary fire hall. The same new council used its first motion day to start undoing the last term’s decisions and to back a look at saving 118 Downtown Eastside rooms. Downtown office vacancy also rose to 13.1 per cent after Amazon consolidated into The Post.

### Top Stories
**Chinatown green space at Gore and Union becomes a permanent park: Daily Hive**
On Tuesday, November 17, 2026, Vancouver city council approved permanent park status for about 31,000 square feet, roughly one acre, of city-owned land at 722 Gore Avenue, on the northeast corner of Gore Avenue and Union Street. Until the vote, the triangle was still set aside for road use, kept as right of way for a highway on-ramp in the 1960s and early 1970s freeway plan between downtown and Highway 1. The Dunsmuir and Georgia viaducts were the only completed piece of that plan. The Vancouver Park Board now has authority over the space. Crews have maintained the informal green for decades, and the trees include a giant sequoia. In 2024 the city proposed a temporary fire hall there to help Firehall No. 2 with Downtown Eastside call volume. Residents fought that plan. Staff withdrew it and used 1756 East Hastings Street instead. Fire Hall No. 11 opened there in spring 2025, and there are directions to redevelop 496 Alexander Street as a permanent, expanded Fire Hall 2. Mayor Pete Fry, then a councillor, brought an October 2024 motion on permanent park status for 722 Gore and the strip north along Gore to Keefer Street. Park Board commissioner Tom Digby had a similar motion approved in September 2024. Tuesday’s designation covers only the triangle, not that strip to Keefer. Fry said people in Strathcona, Chinatown and the Downtown Eastside have used the green space for years, and that protecting it means it stays for people who use it. Digby, the board chair, said the designation was a coordinated effort between the Park Board and council. No formal name or park improvements are planned. Under existing policy, a permanent park designation can be removed only if council and the Park Board each pass a resolution with at least 66 per cent approval of all elected members. The site sits just north of the new St. Paul’s Hospital, set to open in February 2027. Source: [dailyhive.com](https://dailyhive.com/vancouver/722-gore-avenue-vancouver-chinatown-permanet-public-park-designation)

**New council starts reversing the last term and backs a look at 118 SRO homes: Vancouver Sun**
Tuesday’s meeting was the first chance for the new council, a Green, COPE and OneCity coalition, to introduce motions, and many aimed at decisions of the ABC Vancouver council that ran city hall for the previous four years. Green Mayor Pete Fry wants to rescind ABC’s 2023 request that the B.C. government abolish Vancouver’s elected park board. Re-elected OneCity councillor Lucy Maloney wants to reverse the previous council’s 2026 rollback of low-carbon, sustainable building policies. Re-elected COPE councillor Sean Orr wants to revisit ABC’s 2025 freeze on adding new supportive housing. COPE councillor Chloe Leslie introduced an urgent motion on three single-room occupancy buildings in the Downtown Eastside that she said were at imminent risk of receivership, which could put more than 100 low-income tenants at risk of eviction. She told council the Downtown Eastside Community Land Trust had a purchase agreement for all three, set to expire November 18, and that the next foreclosure court date was Friday, covering 118 deeply affordable homes. Her motion directs staff to report by January 2027 on options to support the land trust, including partnerships with senior governments, to communicate urgently with the trust without binding council before that report, and directs the mayor to take the matter to the federal housing minister. Council approved it unanimously. ABC councillor Mike Klassen, the only member of the 11 not in the Green-COPE-OneCity coalition, thanked Leslie and called it a good catch. Speaking outside the meeting, Leslie said she was motivated by concern that when these buildings change hands, new private landlords might pressure tenants to leave. Source: [vancouversun.com](https://vancouversun.com/opinion/columnists/vancouvers-new-city-council-gets-down-to-the-business-of-reversing-last-councils-decisions)

**Amazon’s move into The Post lifts downtown office vacancy to a 22-year high: Daily Hive**
Amazon’s latest consolidation into another part of The Post left about 250,000 square feet empty in two other downtown buildings in the third quarter of 2026, Daily Hive reported, citing CBRE. About 160,000 square feet became vacant in July at the 24-storey Telus Garden tower at 510 West Georgia Street, about 29 per cent of that building’s office space, now leasable from the landlord. Amazon opened its first major Vancouver corporate office there in 2015. Another 90,000 square feet, about 25 per cent of The Exchange at 475 Howe Street, is available for sublease through 2035. CBRE said that move pushed downtown leased-office vacancy from 12.2 per cent in the second quarter to 13.1 per cent in the third, the highest in the city centre in more than 22 years. Across Metro Vancouver, vacancy rose from 11.7 per cent to 12.2 per cent. Outside downtown it rose from 11.2 per cent to 11.3 per cent. Downtown has now been higher than the suburban market for six straight quarters. The regional drop in occupied office space was about 259,000 square feet. CBRE estimates the regional market would have held steady without Amazon’s move, and vacancy stayed under the national average of 16.7 per cent. CBRE expects those large spaces to take time to fill, and sees a later risk of a shortage of premium downtown space because current rents are too low to cover a new downtown tower. It expects no new city-centre supply before 2032 at the earliest. All 492,000 square feet under construction in Metro Vancouver at the end of September was outside downtown. Those two Amazon spaces may be part of Vancouver’s private-sector bid to host the Defence, Security and Resilience Bank headquarters. Formal city bids are due in early December 2026. Amazon began using nearly 600,000 square feet in The Post’s North Tower in March 2026 and has leased 1.1 million square feet across the complex. Source: [dailyhive.com](https://dailyhive.com/vancouver/amazon-downtown-vancouver-office-vacancy-impact-q3-2026)

**Surrey Police Service adds Nyx, its first electronic-storage detection dog: Vancouver Sun**
The Surrey Police Service now has a two-year-old black Labrador retriever, Nyx, trained to find hidden electronic devices that might hold evidence. Her title is electronic storage detection dog, and police say she is the first at a municipal police force in British Columbia. She will work with the cybercrime team. Sgt. Ali Gailus said in a Tuesday news release that dogs like Nyx are trained to detect chemical compounds found in devices such as cellphones, USB sticks, GPS trackers and memory cards, and help locate concealed devices. Deputy Chief Const. Mike Procyk said electronic devices can hold important evidence but are hard to find when deliberately concealed, and that Nyx gives investigators another way to recover it. Indiana-based Jodan Detection K9 trained Nyx and Sgt. Emily Ovington. The money came from a gang violence action fund in coordination with the provincial government. Police say Nyx has already completed six successful searches, and they say digital crime is rising. Source: [vancouversun.com](https://vancouversun.com/news/meet-nyx-the-surrey-police-service-dog-who-finds-electronic-devices) Source: [castanet.net](https://www.castanet.net/news/Metro-Vancouver/638153/Surrey-Police-Service-now-has-an-Electronic-Storage-Detection-Dog) Source: [ca.news.yahoo.com](https://ca.news.yahoo.com/surrey-police-member-sniffs-cybercrime-010642666.html)

### City & Province
**Mayor Doug McCallum repeats a promise to bring racing back to Fraser Downs: Surrey Now-Leader**
At the 11th annual Clovie awards on November 12 at Northview Golf and Country Club, hosted by the Cloverdale District Chamber of Commerce, Surrey Mayor Doug McCallum gave his first public speech since being elected and repeated his promise to rebuild the backstretch barns at Fraser Downs and bring horse racing back to the 5/8 oval in Cloverdale. He said the barns were razed at the end of 2025 under then-mayor Brenda Locke, and that racing was dropped two weeks before the fall meet was to start in September 2025. He said he and the new council directed staff to start on 16 priorities his Safe Surrey Coalition slate committed to, and that the first council meeting approved all 16. He said those include free business licences for the first two years for every new business, freezing property taxes for five years, and free lessons for children 16 and under at city pools. He also pointed to a new swimming pool, a SkyTrain extension to Langley that he said is just about built, and the new hospital in Cloverdale. He said he has had many calls from people who want to open businesses in East Surrey, and that he has heard residents want Cloverdale to keep its small-town character. Indian Chiefs, after the election, warned against ripping up the Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples Act and urged using it as a framework. On the campaign trail the B.C. Conservatives said repealing that act was a top priority. ### The Closer Look
**A 138-year-old Queen’s Park house faces a demolition question: Vancouver Sun**
A New Westminster woman is asking city council to help keep a Victorian Gothic house at 239 Fourth Street, in the Queen’s Park neighbourhood, built in 1888. Marnie Ford says she fell in love with it on night walks. When a for-sale sign went up, she looked for a way to keep the house. She went to council in October and asked the city to buy and restore it, or to help a group of interested people buy and restore it. She said councillors were supportive, and that she is waiting to see whether the new council is as receptive. Mayor Daniel Fontaine and five councillors from the New Westminster Progressives were elected last month on a platform of financial restraint. Only one councillor not affiliated with the Progressives was elected.

The corner lot was listed in August for $1.425 million and can be bought now for $1.25 million. Samuel Boisvert, a director with heritage consultant Luxton and Associates, said the firm was hired to produce a heritage values assessment. The house is owned by the estate of William Shordee, who lived there from 1970 until he died in 2025. Boisvert said the city typically asks for these assessments when the owner of a property older than 100 years wants to develop the site. The house is on the city’s 1986 heritage inventory and is a protected property under the Queen’s Park heritage conservation area, adopted in 2017. It was built in 1888 and got a water hookup in 1893. Boisvert tied that era to an economic boom after the Canadian Pacific Railway arrived in 1886 and built a branch line to New Westminster from Westminster Junction, now Port Coquitlam. Between 1888 and 1892 the city’s population more than doubled, to 7,500. The original lot owner was Methodist minister Edward White, who came to New Westminster in 1859. The lot was once much larger and was subdivided over the years. Boisvert called the house a rare Victorian Gothic example drawing on English and medieval styles.

Rupinder Basi, the city’s deputy director of planning and development, said the owner has asked the city about options related to demolition, and that the city has not received further information about development of the property. Council’s community heritage commission can advise on identifying and protecting heritage buildings. Its role is advisory. Ford’s ask is still a request: a city purchase, or a private group purchase and restoration. The new council has not said which of those, if either, it will take up. Source: [vancouversun.com](https://vancouversun.com/news/138-year-old-heritage-home-in-new-westminster-at-risk-of-demolition)

### Both Sides: A universal tenant-rights bylaw
COPE councillor Sean Orr wants staff to look at a universal tenant-rights bylaw and at criminalizing predatory practices by landlords. The proposal is already drawing a public fight, and council has not voted on it.

COPE, which focused much of this year’s campaign on lower-income people, renters and working people, is using this week’s motions to pursue that platform. Orr’s motion is the piece aimed at landlord conduct: a bylaw covering tenant rights across the city, and a look at treating predatory practices as crimes. The party’s stated reason is the one it campaigned on, improving daily conditions for renters and working people rather than leaving those practices to existing rules alone.

The Goodman Report, a local commercial real estate publication, answered on Monday. It called Orr’s proposal a damaging, ideological policy assault on the city’s landlords and investors, and a governmental sledgehammer that could crush housing investment. That is the case against, as that publication framed it: the cost would fall on people who build and finance rental housing, and the city would scare off investment it needs.

The motions are being introduced this week. The article does not report a vote on Orr’s tenant-rights motion. Source: [vancouversun.com](https://vancouversun.com/opinion/columnists/vancouvers-new-city-council-gets-down-to-the-business-of-reversing-last-councils-decisions)

**Surrey divided on byelection possibility for vacant school board slot: Vancouver Sun**
Garry Thind's Surrey school board seat becomes vacant when he is sworn in as an MLA on Thursday, and Friday is the deadline to ask a court what happens next.

Thind, a realtor, was re-elected last month with the Surrey First Education slate, which has held the board for 12 years. He also won a provincial seat in an election held a week after the local vote. That win disqualifies him from the trustee seat once he is sworn in. Under the Local Government Act, the chief electoral officer, a candidate, or any four electors may apply to the court. A judge can order the position vacant, which could mean a byelection, or declare elected the candidate with the next-highest vote total. Any application must be filed by Friday. The Surrey school district says it is waiting to see whether an application is made and how the court rules. It says a byelection would cost about $840,000, funded entirely by the school district.

If no application is made, a byelection is automatically triggered. If a byelection is not held, Gary Tymoschuk would be reinstated. He was the only Surrey First Education member not re-elected, served 12 years on the board, and his return would keep the slate's majority. Earlier this month, chief election officer Gib van Ert wrote the Municipal Affairs Ministry asking the government to decree the seventh-place finisher elected instead of holding a byelection, according to the Surrey Now-Leader. Trustees now are re-elected Terry Allen, Bob Holmes, Laurie Larsen and Shawn Wilson, with newcomers Michelle Ceniza and Laura Lattanzio, the White Rock representative.

Thind declined to discuss a byelection. He said, "I got disqualified from that position, and so that's my only statement for school board," and that he is "super excited" about the provincial win. Ninth-place finisher Anne Whitmore, president of Surrey's district parent advisory council, who took a leave to run, said she is not applying to the court because of the cost. She and her team do not support giving the seat to Tymoschuk without a byelection. She said the slate ran Thind knowing he had run provincially before and was expected to run again, so a byelection cost was "completely foreseeable." His name stayed on the website, signs and newspaper ads, and social media posts included his name more than 30 times after he announced his MLA candidacy. Whitmore said the province could cover a byelection while pursuing legislative changes, and that "Surrey students should not bear the financial consequences of provincial political decisions." **Canucks ‘More Connected’ as they Put Mammoth on Ice in 3-2 Win: NHL.com**
The Canucks beat the Utah Mammoth 3-2 on Monday for their first back-to-back wins of the season, their second win in as many games. Brock Boeser had a goal and two assists, extending his point streak to eight games, and his power-play winner moved him past Alex Edler for ninth-most power-play points in franchise history, at 178. ### The Closer Look
**Melting glaciers a golden opportunity for one of B.C.'s biggest rock hounds: Vancouver Sun**
Adam Kelliher, 36, spends much of his summers on a mining claim on the peak of Mount Breakenridge, near the northeast corner of Harrison Lake, taking semi-precious stones off ground a glacier used to cover. The Vanderhoof native owns Rubble, Rock and Gems at 250 Southwest Marine Drive in Vancouver, one of the biggest gem and fossil stores in Canada. He says that glacier has receded by at least three metres in the past year, opening virgin pockets of quartz and citrine that weathering and the freeze-thaw cycle have not damaged.

He majored in environmental science at Langara College, with philosophy electives, and told the Vancouver Sun he had to become an artist because neither of those got him a job. Fifteen years later he has left what he calls his starving-artist era. The climate tension is still there. “I was an environmental studies student. So I care about the climate. But at the same time, I’m a bit like, ‘Let’s gooo glacier!,’” he said. He added that he has not “lost my soul where I sold out solely for money.”

Quartz from the King Citrine Mine at Harrison is shot with green needles of actinolite. He says the rare natural yellow citrine often has an amethyst on top — a sceptre he says does not occur anywhere else in the world — and describes a hole a person can sit in, filled with thousands of crystals the size of fingers.

Chloé Monty, a Simon Fraser University master’s student in glaciology, led a study that found the Whistler, Horstman and Blackcomb glaciers have lost between 60 and 95 per cent of their area and are projected to be gone by the turn of the century. She said the Whistler Glacier will likely last a decade, Horstman will vanish in the next 10 to 50 years, and Blackcomb within the next 20 to 70 years. “It was shocking to see how much the glaciers have shrunk when compared to images from the 1970s,” Monty said. “They are shrinking almost in real time when glacier change should be nearly imperceptible on human time scales.”

University of Northern B.C. professor Brian Menounos tracked a faster loss of glacier ice in B.C. and Switzerland with a lidar study, tied to a climate-driven feedback loop. In B.C., soot from wildfires darkens the ice, raises the surface temperature and speeds the melt. Switzerland has lost nearly 20 per cent of its total ice volume in the last five years, with dust from Saharan storms doing similar work. Brent Ward, a professor in SFU’s department of earth sciences, said early spring heat waves now melt the snow quickly, so later summer warmth melts ice directly, worsened here by fire soot. He called that a cascading hazard. Only a few alpine glaciers remain from the Cordilleran ice sheet that covered this region 17,000 years ago and stretched 120 kilometres south of Seattle. Ward said the glacier on Kelliher’s claim looked unhealthy, and the lack of snow on its surface indicated rapid mass loss. In Switzerland, receding ice has uncovered hidden bunkers, munitions and bombs from the First World War. **Canucks defeat Golden Knights to end seven-game skid: NHL.com**
The Vancouver Canucks beat the Vegas Golden Knights 6-3 on Sunday at T-Mobile Arena and ended a seven-game losing streak. Filip Chytil and Linus Karlsson each scored twice. Forward Elias Pettersson scored and had an assist, and Brock Boeser had two assists. Leevi Merilainen made 34 saves on 37 shots in his 12th start in the Canucks’ last 15 games. Vancouver is 4-17-1, and 2-8-0 in its past 10. The team came in with one win in its last 18 games, had not won in regulation since October 3, and had lost eight straight to the Golden Knights. Coach Manny Malhotra said it was really good to hear the win song after a 60-minute effort. Vegas coach Ryan Craig, asked when things went wrong, said “Puck drop.” Jonathan Lekkerimäki set up Pettersson’s power-play one-timer for the first goal. Chytil’s first goal of the night was his first since October 16, 2025, against Dallas; his second was the first short-handed goal of his career, off a stretch pass from Jamie Oleksiak. Mark Stone’s power-play goal was his 417th point with Vegas, tying Jonathan Marchessault for the franchise record, and Drew O’Connor answered 24 seconds later. Karlsson’s empty-net goal closed it. Carter Hart made 21 saves. Vegas is 13-6-3, and a six-game point streak ended. Pettersson has 23 points in 22 games; Boeser has 20. Sportsnet told Offside it is working with other Canadian distribution partners so TV subscribers have more ways to reach Sportsnet+ content. Vancouver’s first Monday Night Hockey game was November 9, a 3-1 Flyers win at Rogers Arena. ### Both Sides: City promises and municipal limits
What is in dispute is not one bylaw vote today. It is whether the promises new Metro Vancouver mayors made — a four-year property-tax freeze, a police helicopter, pools, SkyTrain expansion — are work these councils can do, or pledges that sit outside city money and city powers. The Vancouver Sun reports that two-thirds of the region’s 21 mayors are first-timers, including nine who defeated incumbents.

Surrey Mayor Doug McCallum’s case is that voters hired the council to act. On Monday, a new council made up almost entirely of his Safe Surrey Coalition adopted 16 priorities, including a property-tax freeze, SkyTrain expansion and buying a police helicopter, plus aerial drones for police, four new community swimming pools, and an end to some recreation fees and business licences, all while freezing property taxes for four years. “The people of Surrey did not elect this council to study things. They elected us to get things done,” McCallum said. “Every commitment we made during the election is now a priority of council.” Langley Township Mayor Jay Lundgren, at his November 2 swearing-in, said voters “asked for change,” and “It’s here,” “because something had gone wrong with the way this place was being run.” Vancouver Mayor Pete Fry, who upset Ken Sim, told mostly rookie councillors, “We’re going to do things a little differently,” and warned of turbulence.

Surrey Coun. Harry Bains, the only opposition councillor, questioned whether some of those priorities are appropriate or achievable. “I haven’t seen a request from the police board for a helicopter,” he said, and said city hall needs to separate itself from the operational management of the Surrey police board. Burnaby Mayor Mike Hurley, re-elected to a third term as an independent who must work with eight party-aligned councillors, said several mayoral candidates campaigned on health or education, which provincial or federal governments oversee. “I think we need to be very careful about not kidding ourselves that we can make big changes,” he said. “It’s important that local government learn to stay in their lane.” Former North Vancouver City mayor Darrell Mussatto, mayor from 2005 to 2018, said, “The reality is it’s much more difficult than you realize,” and that big-ticket promises are easy to make and harder to keep. New Westminster Mayor Daniel Fontaine, who ousted an incumbent, said cities collect just pennies of every tax dollar and are financially limited, though his council passed a 100-day plan to add garbage bins, repair sidewalks, ease traffic bottlenecks and eliminate restaurant patio fees. Source: [vancouversun.com](https://vancouversun.com/news/new-metro-vancouver-mayors-campaign-promises)

> **Seven hundred jobs, not three thousand five hundred, now frame Vancouver's defence-bank bid.**

**What You Need to Know:** Seven hundred jobs, not three thousand five hundred, now frame Vancouver's defence-bank bid. ### Top Stories
**Global defence bank headquarters office sought by Vancouver could grow to 500,000 sq. ft.:** Daily Hive Vancouver
Ottawa opened a formal competition on November 13 for the Canadian city that will host the Defence, Security and Resilience Bank, and only Canadian municipalities may apply, with proposals due December 3. The bank is expected to start with about 50 employees and could grow to about 700 within 10 years, in offices that could expand from about 7,500 square feet to about 500,000, far below earlier estimates of as many as 3,500 staff. Canada was unanimously backed as host country in April; Canada and partners are due to sign the Articles of Agreement in Luxembourg on November 30, with operations aimed at 2027 and a European hub also in Luxembourg. Finance Minister Francois-Philippe Champagne said hosting would put a Canadian municipality at the centre of an institution supporting collective security, defence industries and more resilient supply chains. Vancouver’s private-sector bid, which the province and the city backed in February through the Pacific Security Bank Bid Committee, has identified Telus Garden — about 160,000 square feet Amazon vacated in July, plus an 88,000-square-foot sublease — and about 90,000 square feet at The Exchange. Premier-designate Lorne Doerkson called Vancouver a natural choice and said his government stands ready to champion it with industry and federal partners. Doug Guzman, chief executive of Canada’s Defence Investment Agency, will shortlist bids for the prime minister and the finance minister; no date is set for naming the city. Source: [dailyhive.com](https://dailyhive.com/vancouver/dsrb-defence-security-resilience-bank-vancouver-federal-bidding-process-begins)

Four people are facing charges in the killing of a 28-year-old man in Maple Ridge in May, the Integrated Homicide Investigation Team said Saturday. Charles Thomas Shields, 25, is charged with one count of first-degree murder. Meghan-Lynn Jean Nagle, 43, Jason Matthew Bauer, 40, and Samantha Jennifer Garnett, 47, are each charged with one count of manslaughter. Maple Ridge RCMP were called to the 22300 block of Rover Road just before 7 p.m. on May 30 and found the man with life-threatening injuries; he was pronounced dead at the scene. The four were arrested Friday. Sergeant Freda Fong of IHIT said it was a tragic loss of life and that the charges are a significant step in the judicial process. Police say they believe the incident was isolated and that the victim and the accused were known to each other. Source: [globalnews.ca](https://globalnews.ca/news/12151333/4-charged-maple-ridge-homicide/) Source: [surreynowleader.com](https://surreynowleader.com/2026/11/14/four-charged-in-mays-fatal-stabbing-in-maple-ridge/)

Former Conservative leader John Rustad said a fall sitting should pass the promised tax cuts, including a rollback of the provincial sales-tax expansion onto professional services that Premier David Eby moved from October 1 to January 1, 2027, and a rise in the basic personal exemption from $13,216 to $32,000, a cut of up to $1,000 a year that economists have criticized as cutting revenue by up to $4 billion against a $13.8 billion deficit. Former premier Christy Clark said the tax cuts might be the only bill finished besides a throne speech, that many incoming ministers already know the files as critics, and that an early session could be fairly uneventful while the NDP regroups. **Vancouver woman faces forfeiture of goods police allege were stolen and offered for sale online:** Vancouver Sun
B.C.’s director of civil forfeiture has sued in B.C. Supreme Court to take 124 items of clothing, jewelry and accessories that police seized from a Vancouver condo, alleging they were obtained through unlawful activity. The claim, filed this week, names Dana Rosen and alleges she knowingly acquired, stored and trafficked property obtained by crime, and that she failed to take reasonable steps to avoid receiving or selling it.

The director’s case rests on a privately employed investigator who, between December 2025 and May 7, 2026, reported 150 active online listings tied to Rosen’s profile and identified about 1,500 items, totalling about $158,800, as already sold. He told police many of the goods had come from stores in the Vancouver region. He bought two listed items, later confirmed them stolen, and contacted police. Vancouver police undercover officers in the anti-fencing and theft identity unit then bought listed items, including at least one the investigator identified as stolen. Some goods were still in original packaging, some still carried anti-theft tags, and some had serial numbers tampered with or removed, the lawsuit says. It does not say who hired the investigator.

In May, police obtained a warrant and searched a third-floor condo in a three-storey walkup above retail stores on Macdonald Street near West Broadway, and a storage locker tied to the unit. The investigator also identified seized items as stolen, the claim says. The director alleges Rosen bought goods from sellers she knew to be prolific property offenders, used sale proceeds to buy more stolen goods, and did not have sufficient legitimate income to have acquired the merchandise lawfully. The claim says that conduct is illegal under the Criminal Code as possession and trafficking of stolen property over $5,000 and laundering proceeds of crime, and as a failure to declare taxable income under the Income Tax Act. It says Rosen was arrested for possession and trafficking of property obtained by crime. It does not say whether she was charged. The allegations are unproven in court. # Vancouver Daily News
> **Eight hundred Delta Amazon workers now have North America's first imposed union contract.**

**What You Need to Know:** Eight hundred Amazon workers in Delta now have North America's first imposed union contract, after a B.C. arbitrator made the deal binding. Ottawa is putting $200 million into Woodfibre LNG over three years. Surrey's police service is not staffed to take over on schedule, so RCMP members are being asked to cover gaps on voluntary overtime.

### Top Stories
**B.C. arbitrator imposes 1st union contract for Amazon workers in North America: CBC British Columbia**
A B.C. arbitrator has imposed the first union contract for Amazon workers in North America, and the workforce it covers is in Delta. A union representing about 800 Amazon workers there says those workers are now covered by the first binding collective agreement for the retailing giant's employees anywhere in North America. The union is the party making that claim; the CBC report frames the deal as imposed, not negotiated to a voluntary signature. Castanet carries the same development as a contract imposed in B.C., the first of its kind for Amazon workers on this continent. For the Delta group, the change is that a collective agreement is now in force rather than still being sought. Source: [cbc.ca](https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/british-columbia/amazon-union-contract-b-c-first-north-america-9.7421834?cmp=rss) Source: [castanet.net](https://www.castanet.net/news/Metro-Vancouver/637764/First-union-contract-for-Amazon-workers-in-North-America-is-imposed-in-B-C-)

**B.C.'s Woodfibre LNG gets $200M federal cash injection: CBC British Columbia**
The federal government is investing $200 million in British Columbia's Woodfibre LNG project, spread over three years. Energy Minister Tim Hodgson says that funding will help diversify Canada's energy exports. The money is a federal cash injection into a B.C. liquefied natural gas project, attributed by CBC to the minister's export-diversification case. The figure and the three-year window are the concrete change; the stated purpose is Ottawa's, not an independent finding in the report. Source: [cbc.ca](https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/british-columbia/woodfibre-lng-federal-investment-9.7421686?cmp=rss)

**Surrey Police Service doesn't have enough officers to fully take over policing in the city: Yahoo News Canada**
The Surrey Police Service will not be ready to fully take over policing in the city as scheduled, Global News has learned. The service does not have the staffing levels needed for that takeover. RCMP members will have to work voluntary overtime shifts to fill the gaps, which means the municipal force's shortfall is being covered by Mounties choosing extra shifts rather than by a fully staffed Surrey Police Service on the planned date. Catherine Urquhart is the reporter on the Global News account carried by Yahoo News Canada. The practical effect for Surrey is that the scheduled full handover does not happen on the existing timetable because the officer count is not there. Source: [ca.news.yahoo.com](https://ca.news.yahoo.com/surrey-police-doesnt-enough-officers-005734063.html)

**Following federal cuts, Immigrant Services Society of B.C. to close its Richmond branch: CBC British Columbia**
After more than 20 years, the Immigrant Services Society of B.C. says it will close its Richmond branch, and the society ties that closure to federal cuts. CBC describes the shutdown as a major blow in a city where well over half of residents were born abroad. The branch has been open for over two decades; the decision now is to end it. People in Richmond who have used that office for settlement help are the ones who lose the local door, in a municipality the report characterizes by how large its immigrant population is. Source: [cbc.ca](https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/british-columbia/immigrant-services-society-bc-richmond-closes-9.7420991?cmp=rss)

### City & Province
**Adopt-A-School: Meet the ever-growing plight of B.C. schoolchildren: Vancouver Sun**
This year, more than 300 B.C. schools are asking for $2.6 million through the Vancouver Sun's Adopt-A-School campaign. Of that total, $750,000 is the share the schools say they need for grocery cards and food to go home. The rest of the ask sits inside the same $2.6 million figure. The Sun presents the requests as this year's measure of what school communities are seeking for students, with food for home called out as the portion of the total. Source: [vancouversun.com](https://vancouversun.com/news/adopt-a-school-meet-the-ever-growing-plight-of-b-c-schoolchildren)

**Vaughn Palmer: B.C.'s next premier hedges his bets on bridge instead of tunnel: Vancouver Sun**
In a Vancouver Sun column, Vaughn Palmer writes that the B.C. Conservative leader says he is convinced a bridge is cheaper than a tunnel, but is still planning a review before a final decision. That is the leader's stated position, reported as opinion-page news, not a government decision already taken and not a prediction of who forms the next government. The hedge Palmer describes is the review that still sits between the cheaper-bridge conviction and any final call. Source: [vancouversun.com](https://vancouversun.com/opinion/columnists/vaughn-palmer-bc-next-premier-hedges-bets-on-bridge-instead-of-tunnel)

### The Closer Look
**Rangers get four goals in second, top Canucks for fifth win in six games: NHL.com**
The New York Rangers beat the Vancouver Canucks 5-1 at Rogers Arena on Friday, and the game turned in a four-goal second period. Richmond's Glenn Gawdin scored his first two NHL goals in that frame. He is 29, he was playing his 15th NHL game since a debut in 2020-21, and it was his second game with New York after a call-up from Hartford of the American Hockey League on Wednesday, NHL.com reports. He had what he called 10 to 12 family and friends in the stands. "There's a lot that goes through your mind over the years and credit to the circle around me, credit to my wife, they push me when I need it," Gawdin said. "The success tonight, I think they have an equal part in that, so it was a special night." Pacific North Hockey notes he wore number 15, scored the two goals 3:10 apart, and that the second came at 16:10 of the middle period, after Alexis Lafreniere's 10th of the season sat between them. NHL.com times Gawdin's first at 13:00, on a rebound of Leevi Merilainen's clearing attempt that bounced off Filip Chytil. ESPN says the second made it 5-1 with 3:50 left in the period.
Elias Pettersson had opened the scoring at 12:13 of the first, tipping a Zeev Buium point shot, his fifth goal of the season and his first 5-on-5 goal since January 13, ending a 56-game drought at even strength. Gabe Perreault tied it at 18:47. Oliver Bjorkstrand put New York ahead 2-1 on the power play at 8:21 of the second, from J.T. Miller, and Lafreniere made it 4-1 at 15:14 before Gawdin's second. Brock Boeser assisted on Pettersson's goal for his 500th career point — 233 goals and 267 assists — in his 650th game, the eighth player to reach that mark for Vancouver. "Definitely a cool achievement," Boeser said. "It doesn't stop there. Got to keep going, continue to be a leader." Merilainen stopped 25 shots. Dylan Garand stopped 27 for the Rangers; he is from Victoria, played junior in Kamloops, and had an estimated 50 family and friends in the building. Miller had two assists. Pacific North Hockey and Canucks Army both report that the Rogers Arena crowd booed him when he touched the puck. Rangers coach Mike Sullivan credited Miller's corner battle on the tying goal with turning the night. Canucks coach Manny Malhotra said the second period was "a string of turnover after turnover after turnover." Pettersson said the team started well and did not follow it in the second.
The Canucks fell to 3-17-1. They have lost seven straight, they are 1-16-1 in their past 18 games, and Pacific North Hockey puts them at seven points, four behind the Chicago Blackhawks. The Rangers improved to 12-8-1, went 3-1-0 on a four-game road trip, and have won five of their past six. ESPN notes it was New York's first win this season after allowing the first goal; they had been 0-7-1 in that spot. The Canucks play at Vegas on Sunday night. The Rangers host Montreal on Monday night. # Vancouver Daily News
> **From ten to noon, a storm surge may flood low Metro Vancouver shores.**

**What You Need to Know:** From ten to noon, a storm surge may flood low shores in Metro Vancouver, and Environment Canada says the same risk reaches southeast Vancouver Island and the southern Gulf Islands. The agency says high winds and stronger waves could push water above the predicted tide. Most rainfall warnings lifted Thursday after more than 300 millimetres on parts of the southwest, while evacuation orders remain for parts of Pemberton, the Lil'wat First Nation and Zeballos.

### Top Stories
**Rains ease but storm surge heads for southwest B.C.: Global BC**
After this week's storms, the new risk is a storm surge as the rain eases. Environment Canada says the surge could hit low-lying, exposed coastal areas of Metro Vancouver, southeast Vancouver Island and the southern Gulf Islands, with water above tidal predictions driven by high winds and what the agency calls enhanced wave activity, peaking from 10 a.m. to noon. CBC reports the same Friday warning for Metro Vancouver and the Greater Victoria area. Most rainfall warnings that had covered the region were lifted Thursday, though two yellow warnings remain for western and inland Vancouver Island, with the heaviest rain expected near Zeballos and Tahsis into late this afternoon. The drenching has brought more than 300 millimetres to parts of southwest B.C. Residents north of Squamish are sheltering in place. Pemberton remains under an evacuation alert, with parts of the community under an evacuation order, and evacuation orders are also in place for the Lil'wat First Nation and Zeballos. Source: [globalnews.ca](https://globalnews.ca/news/12149350/rains-ease-but-storm-surge-heads-for-southwest-b-c-posing-new-flood-risk/) Source: [cbc.ca](https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/british-columbia/metro-vancouver-greater-victoria-coastal-flooding-9.7420283?cmp=rss) Source: [cbc.ca](https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/british-columbia/metro-vancouver-greater-victoria-coastal-flooding-9.7420283)

**B.C. among Canada's flu hot spots as outbreaks hit long-term care homes: Vancouver Sun**
B.C. has some of the highest influenza activity in Canada, and the virus is linked to multiple outbreaks at long-term care homes across the Lower Mainland. Federal data put B.C. flu activity in the high category, with 17.8 to 27.4 per cent of tests positive at public health laboratories, and only Nunavut ranked higher. Dr. Brian Conway, medical director of the Vancouver Infectious Disease Centre, told Postmedia the spread appears linked to a mutated H1N1 strain of influenza-A that transmits a little more easily, and that people 65 and older are still the majority of cases. Fraser Health lists 12 active influenza outbreaks at long-term care homes, declared between October 23 and November 10. Vancouver Coastal Health lists five flu outbreaks, four at care homes and one at a hospital in Sechelt. A B.C. Centre for Disease Control report published November 4 found 82 of 363 sentinel samples from August 30 to October 24 positive for influenza, a 23 per cent rate, and the centre called activity moderate for October 25 to 31, against low in the comparable week last year. Federal data show 1,699 influenza-associated hospitalizations since August 30, 77 ICU admissions and 31 deaths, with hospitalization data covering 83 per cent of Canadians and ICU and death data covering 22 per cent. Conway said the B.C. vaccine is expected to offer meaningful protection against severe illness from the circulating strain, and that peak protection takes about two weeks. Appointments can be booked at a B.C. pharmacy by calling 1-833-838-2323. Source: [vancouversun.com](https://vancouversun.com/news/bc-among-canadas-flu-hot-spots-as-outbreaks-hit-long-term-care-homes)

**Man shot dead in Surrey: Indo-Canadian Voice**
The Integrated Homicide Investigation Team has been called in by the Surrey Police Service after a man was shot and killed Thursday shortly after 7:15 a.m. at a residence in the 10600-block of 132 Street. Attempts to resuscitate him failed. Surrey Police Sergeant Ali Gailus said officers and B.C. Emergency Health Services were called to the Whalley home at about 7:16 a.m. on November 12 for a man with an apparent gunshot wound, and that he was pronounced dead at the scene. IHIT has taken command. Police are asking anyone with information, CCTV or dash-camera footage to contact the IHIT information line. Source: [voiceonline.com](https://voiceonline.com/man-shot-dead-in-surrey-2/) Source: [theprogress.com](https://theprogress.com/2026/11/12/ihit-called-to-surrey-after-man-shot-dead-at-whalley-home/) Source: [nanaimonewsnow.com](https://nanaimonewsnow.com/2026/11/12/police-investigate-after-man-shot-dead-in-surrey-b-c/)

### City & Province
**There appear to have been senior staff changes at Surrey City Hall: Vancouver Sun**
The City of Surrey website now lists senior-management changes after the election of Mayor Doug McCallum, and the city is refusing to confirm them or say why. Benjie Lee is listed as acting city solicitor, a post held by Philip Huynh before the election. Fire Chief Jason Cairney is also listed as acting general manager of public safety, a post held before the election by Brian Edwards, whom former mayor Brenda Locke appointed in 2025 after he had been in charge of the Surrey RCMP. At a council meeting this week, Huynh, Edwards and city manager Rob Costanzo were absent. Councillor Harry Bains, the only member remaining from Locke's council, said nobody from the mayor or the other councillors had spoken to him about it, and he asked how much severance is being paid, noting Locke's team waited nine months after October 2022 to change the city manager. The city's media relations department told Postmedia it is unable to comment on personnel matters because of privacy and confidentiality. McCallum and deputy mayor Councillor Mandeep Nagra did not respond to questions. An unsigned email to councillors, sent as from Engineering, Planning, Corporate Services and Legal Staff, called the first week absolutely disgraceful and the handling of staff employment borderline criminal. Postmedia emails to Edwards and Huynh bounced back, and an auto-reply said mayor's assistant Harp Dhillon is no longer available. The city's 2025 salary filing lists Huynh at a base of $228,227 plus $52,475 in benefits, Edwards at $99,849 plus $7,844 for a partial year that began at the end of August 2025, Costanzo at a base of $426,821 plus $122,277 in benefits, and Dhillon at a 2025 base of $102,655 plus $14,540. Source: [vancouversun.com](https://vancouversun.com/news/there-may-have-been-senior-staff-changes-at-surrey-city-hall-the-city-wont-talk-about-them)

**Unfinished 24-storey Surrey City Centre condo tower listed for $30 million: Daily Hive**
An unfinished condominium tower at 13862 101 Avenue in Surrey City Centre, built to six storeys of a planned 24, is offered at $30 million in a court-ordered sale. Goodman Commercial is marketing the Centra site for court-appointed receiver Alvarez & Marsal Canada Inc. The 1.2-acre property, about a 13-minute walk from King George Station, was approved for 167 strata homes and 194 parking stalls, and Goodman says more than $23 million has already been spent on hard construction costs, with the asking price about $206 per square foot of approved buildable area. B.C. Assessment's July 2025 roll put the value at $26.71 million. The Supreme Court of British Columbia appointed the receiver in March 2026 over Centra Limited Partnership and other entities linked to the Everest Group. A December 2025 petition from Domain Mortgage Corp., for Capstone lenders, said $27.8 million was advanced in March 2022 at 14 per cent a year and that about $44.2 million was owing, with about $15.2 million in builders' liens on the site. Construction had stopped since late summer 2024. By the March 2026 receivership date, Alvarez & Marsal later reported about $45.7 million owing on the Capstone financing, $8.9 million to Desjardins and $11.5 million to general contractor Metro-Can, which terminated its contract in December 2025 for non-payment. Of 167 homes, 152 had been pre-sold. Those agreements are cancelled, and Goodman is offering the site for a new condominium sales program or for market rental. Source: [dailyhive.com](https://dailyhive.com/vancouver/centra-condo-tower-13862-101-avenue-surrey-court-ordered-sale)

### The Closer Look
**City of Vancouver staff urge rejection of 15-storey downtown hotel: Daily Hive**
City of Vancouver staff want the new council to reject a 15-storey hotel at 852-872 Seymour Street, a mid-block lot between Robson and Smithe across from the Orpheum. Council considers the referral report on November 17. In a rare move, staff recommend a later public hearing and a recommendation to refuse the Bene Group application, designed by Arno Matis Architecture. The plan would keep the historic two-storey front facade of the 1926 Great War Veterans' Association Hall, hold 151 guest rooms, and put a 2,500-square-foot restaurant and bar at street level. The building would be 163 feet tall and about 82,500 square feet, a floor-space ratio of 11 on a lot of roughly 7,500 square feet, with about 18 parking spaces on two underground levels reached by car elevators from the lane.

The previous council protected that facade with a heritage designation in 2023, and staff say the proposed preservation is sufficient. The hall later housed LGBTQ nightclubs, including Playpen Central and Hollywood North. When the neighbouring Marriott tower was approved in 2023, plans for this site contemplated about seven storeys. That 30-storey, 390-room Moxy and Elements project is under construction at 848 Seymour and is expected to open in 2028. Seven of its guest rooms would face only a lightwell on the new hotel's north line. Staff say those rooms would lack enough daylight, sunlight and an outward view, and the Marriott developer has raised significant concerns. To the south, the lot has 62 feet of Seymour frontage and is about 120 feet deep. The design would leave as little as a 36-foot gap to the 29-storey Vita tower at 565 Smithe, built in 2009, short of the typical 60-foot separation from homes that is meant to protect privacy, daylight and sky views. Staff say meeting that standard here would require a lower building. The design uses privacy glass and a climbing-vine wall on the south side. Staff acknowledge the benefit of more hotel rooms, but say this form would create undesirable conflicts with the adjacent hotel and residential sites.

Council can still approve the project. The report includes draft zoning and conditions for that path. A hearing is not legally required, but staff want one because of public feedback and the effect on the two neighbours. Their September 2026 tally says the city is on track for a target of 10,000 net new hotel rooms: seven rezonings under review with 1,480 rooms, 13 approved rezonings with 3,380, four projects with 1,060 in permit steps, six under construction with 1,010, and eight recently completed with 540, about 7,500 rooms in 38 projects. Destination Vancouver estimates 20,000 net new rooms are needed across Metro Vancouver, including 10,000 in the city. About 25,000 hotel rooms exist in the region now, 13,000 of them in Vancouver, fewer than in the early 2000s. Staff say challenging costs leave it uncertain how many approved projects will actually be built. Source: [dailyhive.com](https://dailyhive.com/vancouver/852-872-seymour-street-vancouver-city-staff-hotel-proposal-rejection-recommendation)

# Vancouver Daily News
> **Pemberton's evacuation order shut Airport Road, the airport and the treatment plant.**

**What You Need to Know:** Pemberton's evacuation order shut Airport Road, the airport and the treatment plant, as south-coast rain pushed more communities to move people or cut water use. Surrey's only opposition councillor used the first regular meeting to challenge parts of the mayor's priority list even as those plans advance. Homicide investigators are at a home on East 52nd Avenue after two people were found dead.

### Top Stories
**Impacts from B.C. drenching mount as water levels rise: Global BC**
The Village of Pemberton has issued an evacuation order for properties on Airport Road, including the airport, the wastewater treatment facility, the wildland fire management base and a public golf course, because of flooding and high-risk river levels. The Lil'wat Nation has issued an evacuation order and an evacuation alert from Kwetsa7 along the Lillooet River corridor to Lillooet Lake. On northeast Vancouver Island, the Strathcona Regional District issued a water conservation notice for the Village of Sayward after high flows in Newcastle Creek put extra sediment in the water. An evacuation order for flooding and landslide risk remains in place for about 30 properties in Zeballos, on northwest Vancouver Island. Some areas had a lull on Wednesday, but orange rainfall warnings remain for west and inland Vancouver Island, Howe Sound and the Sea to Sky, with downpours expected today and a risk of significant damage and disruption. In Paradise Valley, a BC Hydro release at the Cheakamus Dam triggered a flood alert, and residents were told to shelter in place. Source: [globalnews.ca](https://globalnews.ca/news/12147625/bc-rainfall-impacts/) Source: [nsnews.com](https://www.nsnews.com/local-news/flood-alert-residents-told-to-shelter-in-place-in-paradise-valley-12935070)

**Surrey's only opposition councillor kicks off term challenging mayor's 16 priority projects: Vancouver Sun**
Coun. Harry Bains, the only councillor not on Mayor Doug McCallum's Safe Surrey Coalition, used Monday's first regular meeting to mark where he stands on 16 priorities the mayor wants implemented. Bains, elected to a second term last month after serving on former mayor Brenda Locke's slate, said he backed items he agreed with and offered amendments on others. Safe Surrey said on social media Tuesday that Bains is against a new hospital, that four years on council delivered no hospital, and that he is playing politics for Locke. Bains said he supports a hospital but wants a women's and children's hospital on a larger site than the three hectares the mayor has offered the province, and he called the slate's portrayal dishonest. He voted against five motions, including a helicopter and drone fleet for the Surrey Police Service unless the police board requests them, and he did not support a four-year property-tax freeze unless McCallum can guarantee it will not cut services, sell city land, cancel budgeted projects, or raise other fees and taxes. Every McCallum plan is still moving ahead, including a call for SkyTrain to Newton, withdrawal from Metro Vancouver, and free licences for two years for every new business. Bains said he worries the money has to come from somewhere, including the 10,000-seat sports and entertainment arena planned for City Centre; McCallum told Postmedia during the campaign he would cancel the arena and has not spoken about it since being elected, and he has not been made available for interviews since election night. Source: [vancouversun.com](https://vancouversun.com/news/only-opposition-surrey-councillor-challenging-mayor-projects)

**Homicide detectives called to Vancouver home after 2 people found dead: Global BC**
Homicide detectives were called to a home in the 1000 block of East 52nd Avenue after officers were first called there around 12:45 a.m. The bodies of a man, 27, and a woman, 35, were found in the home. Source: [globalnews.ca](https://globalnews.ca/news/12146990/homicide-detectives-vancouver-home-2-people-dead/) Source: [vancouversun.com](https://vancouversun.com/news/homicide-investigators-called-in-after-two-people-found-dead-in-vancouver-home)

### City & Province
**Risk of landslides in Cariboo following Pear Lake wildfire: report: CBC British Columbia**
A preliminary report from B.C.'s Ministry of Forests says there is a high risk of landslides, floods and debris flow in parts of the Cariboo after a massive wildfire earlier this year. The assessment covers the area affected by the Pear Lake wildfire. The warning is aimed at people living in those parts of the region. Source: [cbc.ca](https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/british-columbia/cariboo-pear-lake-wildfire-risks-9.7417384?cmp=rss)

**New Coquitlam mayor cites affordability, safety as top issues at inauguration: Tri-Cities Dispatch**
New Coquitlam mayor Hodge used the inauguration to name affordability and safety as the top issues. Tri-Cities Dispatch reported the remarks as he took office. Source: [tricitiesdispatch.com](https://tricitiesdispatch.com/hodge-coquitlam-mayor-inauguration/)

### The Closer Look
**VIDEO: Langley City service especially meaningful – emcee: Surrey Now-Leader**
More than a thousand people filled Douglas Park in Langley City on Wednesday for the Remembrance Day ceremony at the cenotaph. Almost two hours earlier, Cliff Talerico had sat alone on a bench, watching the birds and wondering whether days of torrential rain would keep the crowd small. The rain had stopped. The sky stayed overcast and grey. At first only a few dozen people, mostly cadets and RCMP officers, stood near the bandshell. The park then filled.

Talerico, 84, a Langley City resident, told the Langley Advance Times he enlisted at 17 with his parents' support, mostly because he wanted to get out of Golden. After training he spent three years with the infantry in a small German village, two years in Victoria, and six months in Cypress and the Middle East, then joined the 3rd Field Engineer Squadron based in the eastern Fraser Valley. He served 12.5 years and left in 1972, when his brother Jack talked him into building houses in Chilliwack. He is not a Legion member and does not know many other local veterans. Each year he polishes his shoes, puts on dress pants, a blue blazer with service medals and a green beret with an engineers pin, and walks a few blocks to the City cenotaph. He said he was fortunate not to have seen battle or lost close friends. He was escorted to a seat in front of the cenotaph with a few dozen other veterans.

Sandy Dunkley, a long-time Langley resident, had worried attendance would be low. By the end of the service she said her heart was full, glad that so many still took the time. Emcee Chris Parsons led two minutes of silence. The service included The Last Post, Lament and Rouse, O Canada, God Save the King, In Flanders Fields, prayers and scripture. Parsons spoke about his family's recent trip to Normandy and about Jim McGregor, who led the Douglas Park ceremonies for years before his death earlier this year. Parsons said the day was especially meaningful because those were huge shoes to fill.

He asked the crowd to honour Langley's Pte. Hayden Lykkemark, who answered the call to serve and, with three other members of the Canadian Forces, died last month in an incident at CFB Wainwright. Among 41 wreaths laid at the City cenotaph, two were placed beside flowers and pictures of Lykkemark that have been there since his death. Parsons said Lykkemark will be laid to rest locally next week, and he asked that the service of those now serving, those who served, and those who died not be forgotten. In North Vancouver, the family of Pte. Aidan Goulding, killed in a fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright last month, laid a wreath in his honour. Source: [surreynowleader.com](https://surreynowleader.com/2026/11/12/video-langley-city-service-especially-meaningful-emcee/) Source: [nsnews.com](https://www.nsnews.com/local-news/photos-north-vancouver-holds-solemn-remembrance-day-ceremony-13007742)

**As more people turn to subsidized vet care, several non-profits say they can't meet the demand: CBC British Columbia**

### Sports
**Canucks Place Ilya Safonov on Waivers for Contract Termination: BVM Sports**
Vancouver placed Ilya Safonov on unconditional waivers to terminate his contract after the forward left the Abbotsford AHL affiliate and returned to KHL club Ak Bars Kazan. Safonov said his inability to earn an NHL roster spot factored into the decision, and a larger role at centre awaits in Kazan. He had signed a one-year, $950,000 contract, recorded 4 points in 12 games with Abbotsford, and posted a career-high 37 points in 64 games for Kazan in 2022-23. The return ends a North American stint of five months after six years in Kazan's system. Source: [bvmsports.com](https://bvmsports.com/2026/11/12/canucks-place-ilya-safonov-on-waivers-for-contract-termination/) Source: [prohockeyrumors.com](https://www.prohockeyrumors.com/2026/11/canucks-place-ilya-safonov-on-unconditional-waivers-for-contract-termination.html)

The New York Rangers visit the Vancouver Canucks Friday at 9 p.m. EST. The Canucks are 3-16-1 overall and 1-8-0 at home; the Rangers are 11-8-1. Mika Zibanejad scored two goals in New York's 3-1 win over Calgary. The Rangers won the earlier meeting 6-2, with Will Cuylle scoring twice. Thatcher Demko is out with a hip injury; Tom Willander is day to day with a lower-body injury; Mackenzie MacEachern and Filip Chytil are also out. ### Both Sides: Municipal density rules
Premier-designate Lorne Doerkson has to decide what the new government does with Bills 44 and 47, the two cornerstones of a cabinet-approved 28-point housing plan released in April 2023. Bill 44 gives owners in municipalities over 5,000 the right to build three to six units without a rezoning hearing if they comply with the official community plan. Bill 47 allows much higher density in 104 transit-oriented areas in 31 municipalities.

Gord Enemark, who led the cross-ministry team that built that plan while executive director of the housing policy branch, writes in the Vancouver Sun that the case for staying the course is supply. He writes that staff believed the province could not, alone, pay for tens of thousands of non-market homes and had to use the private sector. Economist Mike Moffatt of the University of Western Ontario, quoted in the December 5, 2023 Globe and Mail, said B.C. was "far ahead of anyone else when it comes to ambition and policy seriousness" and that the whole package, not one silver bullet, was what impressed him. UBC housing economist Thomas Davidoff co-authored a study that concluded the policy should generate over 200,000 new units over 10 years, after researchers looked at similar New Zealand measures from 2016. Enemark's own reason is price and form: a duplex, fourplex or townhouse will always cost less than a single-family house in the same neighbourhood, and most families need ground-oriented housing rather than a condo ten storeys up. He adds that federal housing-accelerator grants could be at risk, because communities over 10,000 must commit to at least four units per property to qualify, and over $500 million has been approved for B.C., most of it for 19 larger municipalities.

The case for slowing down is that the new government should not treat those bills as settled. The Victoria Residential Homebuilders Association told Doerkson he needs to pump the brakes, while saying Bill 44 has increased missing-middle homes 47 percent in Greater Victoria, homes it calls critical for young families. The B.C. Real Estate Association recommends the new government carefully consider its actions on Bills 44 and 47. Business in Vancouver reports that real estate industry groups want housing policies revisited, including tax changes and lower construction costs, to revive development. Enemark names the tradeoff himself: local input through long public rezoning hearings, generally dominated by people who already own housing, is given up so others have more options than they have now. No dated next step is set. Source: [vancouversun.com](https://www.vancouversun.com/opinion/op-ed/opinion-why-the-bc-government-should-tread-carefully-regarding-municipal-density-legislation) Source: [vancouversun.com](https://vancouversun.com/opinion/op-ed/opinion-why-the-bc-government-should-tread-carefully-regarding-municipal-density-legislation) Source: [biv.com](https://www.biv.com/news/real-estate/industry-leaders-urge-new-bc-government-to-revisit-housing-policies-12998747)

# Vancouver Daily News
> **More than $36 million unpaid puts Westbank’s Alberni site under a court receiver.**

**What You Need to Know:** A B.C. Supreme Court order puts a limited receiver over Westbank-linked companies at 1668-1684 Alberni Street after they failed to repay more than $36 million to the Bank of Montreal, with a court sale able to start February 13, 2027. The B.C. Real Estate Association forecasts a modest 2027 rebound in Metro Vancouver and Fraser Valley sales, with prices rising more slowly. Remembrance Day brings holiday transit, free rides for veterans, and morning bus detours downtown.

### Top Stories
**Court appoints receiver for Westbank project site in Downtown Vancouver: Daily Hive**
Justice Loo of the B.C. Supreme Court has appointed a receiver over companies tied to developer Westbank at 1668-1684 Alberni Street, at Bidwell, after they failed to repay more than $36 million to the Bank of Montreal. The order is limited until February 13, 2027: the companies keep running two occupied rental buildings, but rental income after expenses goes to the receiver now, and the receiver cannot run a sale before that date if the debt is still unpaid. The site holds a 15-storey building from 1980 and a 14-storey building from 1990, 23 strata units in all. Interest has been missed since at least September 2025, a January 2026 repayment demand went unmet, and interest was running at about $5,150 a day, with more than $300,000 accrued since BMO’s August 12, 2026 petition. Council approved a 40-storey, 128-unit luxury condo rezoning in May 2022 with a $44 million public-benefits package, including $37 million in cash meant in part for a new Vancouver Aquatic Centre; a development permit was withdrawn in September 2025, and the ruling refers to a purpose-built rental revision with no formal city application yet. Loo found no evidence of the land’s value or of wasted assets, and still held that prolonged non-payment, no repayment proposal, and BMO’s contract right justified the receiver; Westbank’s warning that a receivership could default other projects was not backed by evidence in court. Guarantors named in the case are 700 Bidwell Limited Partnership, 700 Bidwell Property Inc., and Westbank Holdings Ltd., beside borrower 700 Bidwell Holdings Inc. Source: [dailyhive.com](https://dailyhive.com/vancouver/1668-1684-alberni-street-vancouver-westbank-receiver-court-ruling)

**Metro Vancouver and Fraser Valley home sales forecast to rebound in 2027: Daily Hive**
The B.C. Real Estate Association’s fourth-quarter forecast, out today, expects home sales in Metro Vancouver and the Fraser Valley to rise by roughly nine per cent in 2027 after another declining year. Province-wide, it puts 2026 at just over 67,000 sales, down 4.5 per cent from 70,186 in 2025, then 71,840 in 2027, up 7.2 per cent. Chief economist Brendon Ogmundson said a modest recovery should follow as the impact of new United States tariffs fades and fixed mortgage rates decline, while active listings sit near the highest level since 2015. Greater Vancouver Realtors’ average price is forecast at $1.223 million in 2026 and $1.25 million in 2027; the Fraser Valley board’s average is forecast to fall 4.8 per cent to $962,900 in 2026, then rise to $980,000 in 2027, still about $31,800 below 2025. On October 28 the Bank of Canada raised its policy rate by 0.25 percentage points to 2.5 per cent, the first increase since July 2023, citing inflation concerns from oil prices tied to the U.S.-led war in Iran, with its next decision set for December 9. Source: [dailyhive.com](https://dailyhive.com/vancouver/bcrea-metro-vancouver-fraser-valley-housing-market-forecast-2027)

**What's open and closed on Remembrance Day 2026 in Metro Vancouver: Vancouver Sun**
Remembrance Day is a statutory holiday today, and many Metro Vancouver malls are opening after the eleventh hour, generally from 11:05 a.m. to 7 p.m., with Park Royal at 11:15, the Amazing Brentwood at 10:50 for an indoor ceremony, and Willowbrook closing at 6. Costco stores across the region are open; Ikea in Coquitlam and Richmond runs 10 a.m. to 9 p.m.; McArthurGlen is 10 to 8 and Tsawwassen Mills 11:05 to 7. Most community centres are closed, with a short list on statutory hours; most pools stay open except Kensington; libraries are closed except Carnegie; ice rinks and the Fraserview, Langara, and McCleery golf courses are open. TransLink buses, SkyTrain, and SeaBus run holiday schedules, veterans and serving members ride free with ID, badge, service card, or uniform, an accessible fare gate stays open from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m., other riders need only a one-zone fare, and the West Coast Express is not running. Vancouver and Surrey city halls, Service Canada, passport offices, and ICBC are closed and due back Thursday; Canada Post is not collecting or delivering mail today. Regular transit hours and fares resume November 12. Source: [vancouversun.com](https://vancouversun.com/news/remembrance-day-2026-whats-open-closed-metro-vancouver) Source: [princegeorgepost.com](https://www.princegeorgepost.com/news/remembrance-day-2026-whats-open-closed-metro-vancouver)

**Chilliwack veteran, 95, recalls dangerous journey to Korean War: Surrey Now-Leader**
Leroy George, 95, of Chilliwack, told an Indigenous veterans ceremony Friday at the K'ómoks First Nation Gym in Courtenay that he married Ruthie on August 7, 1950, after promising he would not enlist, and joined within a week. On the train from Shilo, Manitoba, toward Fort Lewis, he gave up a card seat to soldier Basil Patrick McKeown minutes before the Canoe River crash, which killed 21 people, including 17 soldiers, McKeown, and George’s cousin Austin Emery George. Ruthie was told he was dead, then, after a roll call at Wainwright, Alberta, that he was alive. He served 11 months in Korea, was wounded in the right eye by a shell, and served 40 years in all. “War is hell,” he said. “It’s boring 90 per cent of the time, and 10 per cent of just hell.” Source: [surreynowleader.com](https://surreynowleader.com/2026/11/11/chilliwack-veteran-95-recalls-dangerous-journey-to-korean-war/)

### City & Province
**'Is this the best we can do?': B.C. mom of boy with muscular dystrophy calls for rare disease strategy: Vancouver Sun**
Kasha Mitton, a Kamloops nurse, is in Vancouver this week for the Till and McCulloch Meetings, asking for a national rare-disease strategy so children can reach drugs already approved but still stuck in provincial funding review. Her son Jude, now 14, was diagnosed at four with Duchenne muscular dystrophy; he can no longer walk, which she says cuts his chances of trials that want patients who are still ambulatory. He had been in a trial for vamorolone, the first Duchenne treatment approved in Canada and commercially available since April, which the family still cannot get in B.C. because funding approval is unfinished. They moved to a trial of givinostat, which University of B.C. professor Fabio Rossi says can slow the disease and is in priority review at Health Canada. The Canadian Organization for Rare Disorders says only 60 per cent of rare-disease treatments reach Canada, most up to six years later than in the United States. “We don’t have time to wait. Time is muscle,” Mitton said. Source: [vancouversun.com](https://vancouversun.com/news/bc-mom-of-boy-with-muscular-dystrophy-calls-for-rare-disease-strategy)

**'Good fire': Indigenous stewards advocate for more controlled burns to combat wildfire in B.C.: CBC British Columbia**
Indigenous fire practitioners and researchers are pressing to put strategic, low-intensity burns back on the land outside peak wildfire season. They say those fires protect communities by taking away fuel future fires would use, and that they leave healthier landscapes. The work is aimed at forest management across British Columbia, not at a single burn scheduled for today. Source: [cbc.ca](https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/british-columbia/indigenous-cultural-burning-forest-management-9.7415060?cmp=rss)

### The Closer Look
**Federal budget's $1.3 billion for Eastern Canada ferries sparks calls for more BC Ferries funding: Daily Hive**
The BC Ferry and Marine Workers’ Union wants Prime Minister Mark Carney to explain why last week’s 2026 federal budget assigns $1.3 billion to ferry services in Eastern Canada and no matching sum to BC Ferries. That money runs over eight years from the 2026/2027 fiscal year, renewing the Ferry Services Contribution Program, including new terminals at Wood Islands, Prince Edward Island, and Caribou, Nova Scotia, plus charters for temporary replacement vessels. Union president Eric McNeely said the prime minister wants to build a stronger, more connected Canada, then added, “Apparently, that doesn’t include the Pacific coast.”

The comparison sits on a 1977 agreement, updated in 2005/2006. Transport Canada expects B.C. to receive $37.8 million in 2025/2026 and $39.05 million in each of 2026/2027, 2027/2028, and 2028/2029, with an evaluation set for 2027/2028. The union says Ottawa covers about 43 per cent of operating and maintenance costs for Atlantic ferry services and about three per cent for BC Ferries. Marine Atlantic’s year-round North Sydney to Port aux Basques run, and the Confederation Bridge to Prince Edward Island, meet constitutional links between provinces. BC Ferries, owned by the province and no longer a Crown corporation after 2003, has said its federal infrastructure financing must be repaid, unlike eastern grants and operating funds.

Fares here are already in front of a regulator. In late 2024, BC Ferries leadership warned that operating, labour, and capital costs could equal a single-year increase of up to 30 per cent in 2028. That was a warning, not an approved fare. The commissioner is reviewing the submission for the four years from April 2028. Through March 2028, average annual increases stay capped at 3.2 per cent, after a $500 million provincial contribution in 2023 that avoided a 10.4 per cent hike each year from 2024 to 2028. The network carried about 23.3 million passengers and 10 million vehicles in the year ending March 2026. The union estimates about $8 billion in cargo a year and says higher fares would hit businesses that depend on the ships, and Vancouver Island’s roughly one million residents. McNeely wants premier-elect Lorne Doerkson to press Ottawa for a larger share. On October 26, 2026, the board replaced CEO Nicolas Jimenez with interim leader Brian Anderson and opened a Revitalization Review, without a public reason. Four Summit-class ships, the fleet’s largest capital project at well over a billion dollars, are due from 2029 to 2031 on the major routes from Metro Vancouver to Vancouver Island and the Sunshine Coast, built at a mainland China yard owned by the Chinese government. Source: [dailyhive.com](https://dailyhive.com/vancouver/canada-federal-budget-eastern-canada-bc-ferries-funding-criticism)

### Also Today
